verdict_reason: Every methodological ingredient of the BENCH proposal exists in print, in other fields' vocabulary: (1) CV-based CIs and tests for the difference between two learners with correlated folds (Nadeau-Bengio 2003; Bates-Hastie-Tibshirani 2024; Bayle et al. NeurIPS 2020; Bayle-Janson-Mackey ICML 2026, which shows such inference can fail for relatively unstable comparisons); (2) a subject-as-population-unit estimand for model comparison with few subjects and a documented small-N correction (Schutt-Kriegeskorte et al. eLife 2023: cross-validated 2-factor bootstrap, inflated false positives below ~20 subjects, n/(n-1) correction); (3) clustered SEs, paired model differences and power/minimum-detectable-effect formulas for benchmark comparisons (Miller 2024, LLM evals); (4) leave-one-cluster-out / internal-external CV with random-effects meta-analysis, prediction intervals and few-study HKSJ corrections for comparing prediction models across a few clusters (Debray, Riley, Snell et al.; Rover-Knapp-Friede); (5) few-cluster-valid intervals (Cameron-Miller, CR2/Bell-McCaffrey, wild cluster bootstrap) and multiplicity/aggregation across tasks (Demsar; Corani-Benavoli Bayesian hierarchical correlated t-test; Longjohn-Gopalan-Casleton 2025). I found no paper that applies this to HEST-Bench or any pathology-foundation-model-on-ST benchmark with donors as the replication unit: HEST-1k reports SD across folds only, STP-Bench (Sept 2026) runs no inferential comparison of encoders, other ST/PFM papers use gene-wise Wilcoxon + FDR (genes as units), spot- or case-level bootstrap, or an ad hoc hierarchical bootstrap (SpaFactor). The specific application is unclaimed, but the statistical content is not new.

what_remains_open: Open only at the level of application-specific statistical content, not new inferential principles: (a) A precisely stated donor-population estimand for the HEST-Bench metric: expectation over donors of the within-donor per-gene Pearson correlation averaged over a gene panel, and of its encoder difference, under leave-one-donor-out folds with frozen encoder + PCA + ridge head; prior work targets accuracy/AUC/MSE, not a ratio statistic computed within a donor then averaged over a handful of donors, with a gene panel chosen using all samples. (b) Which dependence structure is the replication unit: donors (2-6 in most HEST-Bench tasks) with genes as a fixed correlated panel and spots nested, versus common practice of testing over genes or spots; no retrieved paper quantifies the anti-conservatism on ST benchmarks. (c) A validity study of few-donor intervals (t with G-1 df, CR2/Bell-McCaffrey, wild-cluster, HKSJ, Schutt's corrected bootstrap, sign-flip randomization) for the paired difference of two frozen encoders at G=2-6, where pairs bootstrap and Wald t are known to fail; a specialization of econometrics/meta-analysis results, not a new theorem. (d) A power / minimum-detectable-difference table for HEST-Bench-sized tasks from empirical between-donor variances of paired encoder differences, plus multiplicity across tasks x encoders; Miller (2024) and the Debray-Riley literature give formulae in other settings, HEST-Bench numbers are not in the literature I retrieved. (e) A theoretical piece, if wanted: whether the Bayle-Janson-Mackey relative-stability condition holds for ridge heads on near-identical frozen embeddings with donor-level folds; a different claim from BENCH as stated.
sharpened_claim_if_any: Donor-level inference for encoder comparisons on HEST-Bench-type tasks: with the donor (not spot, gene or fold) as replication unit, report the paired difference in donor-mean per-gene Pearson correlation with a few-donor-valid interval (t_{G-1}/CR2 or sign-flip randomization), show by simulation seeded with real embeddings and empirical between-donor variances that SD-over-folds and gene/spot-level tests are anti-conservative at G<=6, and give minimum-detectable-difference tables for the nine HEST-Bench tasks. Frame as an empirical benchmarking-methodology result, not a new inferential method.
value_assessment: Blunt: as a methods contribution for a top statistics journal or NeurIPS/ICML/AISTATS, no. The machinery is a re-assembly of known results (cluster-robust paired CIs, HKSJ/CR2/wild bootstrap for few clusters, nested-CV and Nadeau-Bengio corrections, Holm/BH or Bayesian hierarchical aggregation, power formulas), several in Miller (2024), Schutt et al. (2023) and the clinical-prediction IECV literature in nearly this form; a reviewer would call it an application of known tools. What is not in the literature I retrieved is the empirical HEST-Bench finding (how many donors separate UNI/H-optimus/ResNet50-class encoders); PFM benchmark papers already hint at overlapping CIs and small task-dependent differences, so the result is unsurprising. It could support a short applied paper (NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks, a Bioinformatics/Genome Biology-type benchmarking note, a workshop paper) or a section of the PPI paper. A stats-methods paper would need a new theoretical piece, e.g. validity of CV-difference inference under donor-level folds for frozen-feature ridge heads in the relative-stability regime, or design-based estimand theory for a ratio statistic over few donors; I found none in the literature but did not test whether it would be non-trivial. It is also off-axis from the labelling-budget PPI paper.

verdict_reason: No single paper found that does the full proposal (cluster-level head trained on labelled clusters' mean embeddings, shrunk toward the within-cluster coefficient, with label-free Pi-geometry, inside PPI, with a floor theorem). But every load-bearing piece is already published, and the method is a direct instantiation of existing frameworks once clusters are treated as the units: (1) Whole-cluster PPI/regression estimator = iid PPI on G cluster-level units; its variance depending on the predictor only via cluster means is the cluster-level regression-adjustment identity (Cochran; Su & Ding 2021; Middleton & Aronow; Konrad & Burgard 2026 hybrid GREG states the unit-level vs cluster-level assisting-model trade-off incl. ecological fallacy; Broska & Howes 2610.09601 gives cluster-robust PPI++ variance). (2) 'Train/recalibrate the head on labelled data to minimise PPI variance' is Ji-Lei-Zrnic 2025 (recalibrated PPI, learns optimal imputed loss), Calibeating PPI 2026, GRE-PPI 2026, MoE-PPI 2026, and especially Transfer-Calibrated PPI (2609.34156: adapt a source predictor to the target with a small gold sample via cross-fitting, high-dimensional MSE bounds, guaranteed no worse than PPI++). Pooled-trained head = 'source predictor', cluster-mean fit = 'calibration'. (3) Between block fitted on cluster mean embeddings = distribution regression / multiple-instance regression with a linear kernel (Szabo et al.), and shrinkage toward the within coefficient = ridge toward a source coefficient (Trans-Lasso, random-coefficient transfer ridge, Bastani). (4) The floor ||Pi^{1/2}(beta_B - beta_W)||^2 is the Mundlak/Neuhaus-Kalbfleisch within-vs-between algebra (pooled OLS is a matrix-weighted mix of within and between); Javanmard et al. 2024 prove that instance-level loss = bag-level loss + within-bag-variation regulariser, which is the same ANOVA split for heads. Arkhangelsky-Imbens and Fuhr-Papies use group-mean (Mundlak) features inside flexible/ML nuisance models. Searches: ~133 query executions (104 arXiv API, 14 Crossref, 10 web_search, 5 failed Semantic Scholar) across PPI/ML, econometrics (Mundlak/CRE), survey sampling (GREG/SAE), cluster-randomised-trial causal inference, distribution regression/MIR/aggregate-label learning, transfer ridge, genomics (pseudoreplication). The last two rounds (about 22 queries) yielded no new close paper.

what_remains_open: Honestly narrow. (a) A clean statement, in PPI language, that a head trained by pooled unit-level loss on external/other data carries a variance floor ||Pi^{1/2}(beta_B - beta_W)||^2 for cluster-mean estimands, and that this floor is invariant to the number of spots and does not shrink with more labelled clusters unless the head is re-fitted at the cluster level. I found no PPI/semi-supervised paper that states this; but it is a corollary of the Mundlak identity (pooled coefficient = matrix-weighted average of within and between) plus the cluster-level regression-estimator variance, so it is a proposition, not a theorem. (b) A finite-G, high-dimensional (p >> G_L) oracle inequality for the PPI variance of a Pi-metric ridge head centred at beta_W, fitted on cluster means with Pi estimated label-free from all clusters. TC-PPI gives sparse-lasso bounds for iid units; Zhang-Li give p/n-proportional ridge risk for prediction, not for PPI variance or cluster-level units; nothing found for the combination. This is the only part that could carry technical weight, and it depends on cross-fitting at G_L=4-16, where oracle inequalities are likely to be loose. (c) The empirical question whether the floor is actually binding on ST data. Project evidence (foundation-model heads barely beat a constant predictor on Visium kidney within-donor slopes) suggests weak signal, not within/between conflation, may dominate. NOT verified: forward citations of Ji-Lei-Zrnic, TC-PPI and Broska-Howes (Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429 throughout); papers appearing after the last arXiv listing queries; non-arXiv venues (JASA/Biometrika/JSSAM/Survey Methodology) beyond Crossref title search; I read full text only by keyword scan, not line by line.
sharpened_claim_if_any: If pursued at all, the defensible claim is: 'For PPI with whole-cluster labels and cluster-mean estimands, any head fitted by pooled unit-level loss is variance-suboptimal by exactly ||Pi^{1/2}(beta_B - beta_W)||^2 (Mundlak floor) irrespective of unit count; a Pi-metric ridge head centred at beta_W and fitted on the G_L labelled cluster means with cross-fitting attains PPI variance within an explicit finite-G factor of the best linear head, with Pi estimated from unlabelled cluster means.' Present it as a finite-cluster analysis of recalibrated/transfer-calibrated PPI at the cluster level, and cite Ji-Lei-Zrnic, TC-PPI, Javanmard et al., Mundlak, Su-Ding and Broska-Howes as the frame.
value_assessment: Blunt: as a stand-alone methods paper at a top statistics journal or NeurIPS/ICML, the open remainder is thin. The method reduces to existing recalibrated/transfer-calibrated PPI applied to G cluster-mean units with a ridge prior centred at the pooled head; the floor result is a short corollary of the Mundlak within/between identity; reviewers will see both immediately. What could survive is a rigorous finite-cluster, p >> G_L oracle inequality with label-free Pi-geometry shrinkage, but that is an incremental theory contribution to TC-PPI/Ji et al., and the project's own results (weak predictors on kidney tasks, ratios 0.74-0.84 on lung, 0.6 on census) suggest the practical gain from fixing the head is modest relative to what a constant-plus-power-tuning baseline already delivers. Better used as one section/diagnostic (a 'within-between decomposition' check on whether a head is worth using) inside a larger paper than as the paper's core. A methods venue like AISTATS or a biostatistics applications journal (e.g. Biostatistics, Annals of Applied Statistics) is plausible only if the empirical ST/census gains are clear; JASA/AoS/NeurIPS-level novelty is not supported by what I found.

verdict_reason: Lee & Ren (arXiv:2501.02514, Jan 2025) already do conformal selection with FDR control under exactly the 'donors exchangeable, spots exchangeable within donor' (hierarchical exchangeability) assumption, for test groups M>=1, with two calibration schemes: one random calibration unit per donor (subsampling conformal e-values) and a deterministic donor-weighted (1/N_k) version, aggregated via e-BH. That is claim (i) and the core of claim (iii). The guarantee they give is marginal over the new group (conditional only on group sizes). Pieces of claim (ii) are also anticipated in the neighbouring literature: Duchi-Gupta-Jiang-Sur (arXiv:2403.16336, Sec. 7) show environment-conditional coverage is impossible for prediction sets and that (alpha,delta) guarantees need many environments; Bates et al. (arXiv:2104.08279) separate marginal from calibration-conditional FDR. No retrieved paper proves an FDR-specific donor-conditional impossibility or a K-resolution characterization, and none studies power at K=10-20. I also found no histology/ST method with a selection error-rate guarantee. What remains is a thin extension of an existing framework, not a new framework. Readings: Lee-Ren intro, setup, Thm 1, ITE e-values, simulations, real data and discussion were read; appendix proofs were not.

what_remains_open: (a) A donor-conditional (calibration/new-donor-conditional) FDR statement for conformal selection: an explicit FDR-specific impossibility result (analogue of Duchi et al. Sec. 7, Vovk/Barber et al.) and the matching achievable PAC-type guarantee at rate ~K^-1/2 over calibration donors (analogue of Bates et al.). Lee & Ren list group-feature-conditional FDR as open; I found no paper answering it. (b) A quantitative K-resolution result: with one subsampled unit per donor the conformal p-value has granularity 1/(K+1), so at K=10-20 and alpha=0.1 BH/e-BH can reject only at the extreme; a statement of what power is attainable as a function of K, and whether the all-spots hierarchical e-value or a new aggregation beats the one-spot-per-donor scheme in that regime (Lee & Ren only simulate K=200, M>=20). (c) Using a few labelled spots in the new donor (GHCP-style, arXiv:2608.15500) for selection. (d) The ST-specific piece: spatial dependence inside a donor, and a histology-to-expression application with real donors (HEST-1k) showing FDR/power at K=10-20; no guaranteed-selection method for histology-to-ST was found. Items (a)-(c) are variations on the Lee-Ren / HCP / Bates toolkit; (d) is an application.

This is only worth pursuing if the small-K power gain is large and provable; the validity piece must be framed as a corollary of Lee-Ren.
value_assessment: Blunt: as stated, the claim is not a top-journal or NeurIPS/ICML methods paper. Claim (i) and the central procedures of (iii) are already in Lee & Ren 2025 by authors who also own HCP, batch PI and GHCP, so the validity theory has no novelty and they can write any natural extension quickly. The impossibility result in (ii) is a routine transplant of known conditional-coverage impossibility (Vovk; Barber et al.; Duchi et al. Sec. 7) and the PAC relaxation is a routine transplant of Bates et al.; a referee would likely call it a corollary. What could still be substantive is a sharp small-K power analysis (what power is attainable at K=10-20 as a function of K, alpha and signal) together with a procedure that provably or empirically uses within-donor information to beat subsampling, but I have no evidence yet that such a gain exists, and e-BH with K+1-sized denominators looks intrinsically limited at K=10-20. As a statistics-forward application paper (histology-to-ST selection with finite-sample FDR at K=10-20 donors on HEST-1k, with honest negative results on when it is powerless) it is plausible for a venue like Biostatistics, Annals of Applied Statistics or a biology-methods journal, but not as a theory contribution. Also note the project's own finding that foundation-model predictors add little over a constant on Visium kidney tasks suggests selection power may be near zero on those tasks, which would undercut the application.

verdict_reason: The core phenomenon and the core calibration machinery are already in the literature under FDP/FDX vocabulary. (1) Non-concentration of the proportion of false rejections under strong/pervasive dependence, with a limit determined by the realised factor, is established for FDP: Owen 2005, Delattre & Roquain 2011, Fan-Han-Gu 2012 (FDP given the factor realisation; consistent estimate of realised FDP), Fan & Han 2017 (estimated factors), Kluger & Owen 2024 ('bursty' FDP under many strong long-range correlations). A per-gene interval miss at the true parameter is the same event as a false rejection of a true null, and the all-intervals-evaluated-at-truth FCP is the FDP/number-of-rejections under the global null; Mathur & VanderWeele 2023 literally propose a resampled null interval for the number of alpha-level rejections under correlated outcomes. (2) P(FCP>gamma)<=delta with resampling/sign-flip calibration under arbitrary dependence and few units is the FDX/k-FWER problem: Lehmann-Romano 2005, Romano-Wolf 2007, Delattre-Roquain 2015, Hemerik-Goeman 2018, Hemerik-Solari-Goeman 2019, Hemerik 2025 (finite-sample sign-flip, no large-n requirement). (3) The fixed-calibration-size, many-test-points version of exactly the term 'false coverage proportion' (non-degenerate Beta/Polya-urn limit, in-probability FCP bounds) is Gazin-Blanchard-Roquain 2024 for conformal intervals. I found no paper that does this for PPI / rectifier-based intervals, with few clusters and a pervasive cluster factor, but that gap is a change of setting, not a new idea.

what_remains_open: Only a narrow, setting-specific remainder was not found in anything retrieved: (a) a PPI/rectifier-specific statement: with n_L labelled clusters (4-16), studentised cluster-level rectifier means for hundreds of genes follow a factor model, so conditional on the factor scores the miss events are independent across genes and FCP -> a deterministic function of the realised factor sample (t_{n_L-1}-type, skewed). In the extreme one-factor, vanishing-idiosyncratic-noise case this collapses to FCP in {0,1} with P(FCP=1)=alpha_per_gene, which is an elementary corollary of Fan-Han-Gu-type conditioning, not a theorem needing a paper. (b) Fixed-n_L, large-m asymptotics (HDLSS regime: factor estimable as m->inf with n_L fixed, but not the factor MEAN, so the realised FCP is unidentifiable and only its distribution can be calibrated) for t-statistics with n_L as small as 4 and skewed factors: Fan-Han, Kluger-Owen, Mei-Jiang assume n large or weak/known structure; I found nothing treating n fixed and strong factor with studentisation. (c) Small-n_L feasibility of sign-flip exceedance bounds: 2^{n_L} flips give coarse p-value resolution (16 at n_L=4, 65536 at 16) and sign-flip validity needs symmetry, which the skewed cluster contributions violate; the project's own observation that every design-based interval under-covers at few clusters because the reference distribution is wrong would bite here too. A calibration that remains valid under skew with ~4-16 clusters and gives non-trivial P(FCP>gamma)<=delta would be new as a method, but nothing retrieved shows it is possible; it may be impossible (Bahadur-Savage-type limits) for small n_L. (d) Application to histology-predicted spatial transcriptomics with PPI intervals. Not searched exhaustively: Semantic Scholar forward citations were obtained only for Gazin and Hemerik (Weinstein-Ramdas returned none); Giglio-Liao-Xiu, Notip, and Harvey-Liu-Zhu were seen by title/search record only; no full-text read of Hemerik-Solari-Goeman beyond abstract/intro.
sharpened_claim_if_any: If pursued at all, restate as: 'For few-cluster PPI/rectifier intervals over many outcomes with a pervasive cluster factor, per-outcome (1-alpha) coverage is uninformative about the realised fraction of failures (known: FDP burstiness, Owen 2005; Kluger-Owen 2024; Gazin et al. 2024 for conformal FCP); we show X about whether any distribution-free or sign-flip-type calibration of P(FCP>gamma)<=delta is attainable when n_L<=16 and factor scores are skewed.' The contribution would be a negative/impossibility result or a calibration that survives skew at tiny n_L, not the non-concentration phenomenon or the factor-adjusted/sign-flip recipe.
value_assessment: Blunt: as stated this is not a top-journal methods paper. The non-concentration, the factor-conditional limit, factor-adjusted realised-FDP estimation, sign-flip/permutation exceedance bounds, and even the term FCP with fixed-calibration in-probability bounds (conformal) are all published. A reviewer would see 'FDX/k-FWER for intervals under a factor model, instantiated for PPI rectifiers' and ask what is new; the honest answer today is the instantiation. It could still be a solid applied-methods or workshop contribution (a useful warning that per-gene PPI coverage misleads in ST studies with few donors, with a reporting recipe built from Hemerik/Romano-Wolf machinery) and a good component of a larger paper. It becomes a stats-journal/NeurIPS-grade contribution only if the fixed-n_L, studentised, skewed-factor regime yields a genuine theorem (e.g. exact limit law plus an impossibility or minimax-optimal calibration at n_L=4-16) that the large-n FDP literature cannot give. I would not make it the main thread without that result, and would first test (by simulation, cheaply) whether any sign-flip or factor-adjusted calibration actually achieves P(FCP>gamma)<=delta at n_L<=16 under skew.

verdict_reason: No retrieved paper does the exact thing (gene set as a finite population, measured panel as a possibly prediction-guided unequal-probability sample of genes, difference/HT estimator over genes with design-based intervals for per-spot or per-region signature scores). But every ingredient is prior art in some field: (i) difference/GREG estimator valid under arbitrary predictions (Breidt & Opsomer 2017; 'PPI is the difference estimator' arXiv 2603.19160); (ii) optimal inclusion probabilities proportional to residual SD (Godambe-Joshi 1965, Isaki-Fuller 1982, Zrnic & Candes active inference 2024) which gives the 'optimal panel design' verbatim with unit=gene; (iii) sampling of items/variables from a finite universe with unbiased estimation of the total score and its SE (multiple matrix sampling, Lord & Novick 1968; split-questionnaire designs, Raghunathan & Grizzle 1995, Chipperfield & Steel 2009); (iv) cross-gene error correction for imputed ST (TIDEST, Testa-Lei-Roeder 2026 preprint, debiases imputed genes with residuals of correlated measured genes and names gene-set enrichment as a future extension) and cross-gene conformal calibration (TISSUE, Nat Methods 2024). The gap is a specific instantiation, not a new idea; TIDEST is the nearest threat and could be extended to gene sets by its authors.

value_assessment: Blunt: the open remainder is thin as a statistics-methodology contribution. The estimator is the Cochran/Sarndal difference estimator; the optimal design is Godambe-Joshi/Isaki-Fuller/active inference; the 'items as finite population' framing is multiple matrix sampling and split-questionnaire design; PPI-as-survey-sampling has been written down (arXiv 2603.19160). A top stats journal (JASA/JRSSB/AoS) or NeurIPS/ICML would see an instantiation of known results; the one non-trivial statistical piece would be a variance/inference treatment under strong within-spot gene-gene error dependence and tiny finite populations, plus a theory result about when prediction-guided gene sampling beats uniform, and I did not find evidence these are hard or deep. The strongest honest framing is an applied-methods/genomics paper (Bioinformatics, Genome Biology Methods, or a stats-in-biology venue like Annals of Applied Statistics or Biostatistics) with a randomised-panel-component design and real Xenium/MERFISH benchmarks. Practical obstacle: it requires a new experiment with randomised panels or an assumption of gene exchangeability that existing panels violate, so retrospective validation on public data would be a simulation by masking genes, which weakens the evidence. TIDEST's authors (Lei is a statistician) have already announced gene-set extension as future work, so a scoop risk exists. I would not make this the main paper; at most a secondary application/section if the cluster-level PPI work needs a second ST use case.

The single-group ingredients exist (Dhillon et al. exact expected-size integral via the order-statistic law of the threshold; Yao-He-Gastpar non-asymptotic length bounds in n, m, alpha). Duchi-Gupta-Jiang-Sur (resizing with a few test-environment labels) and Zhang et al. JMLR 2026 (width with limited target data + sources) cover the 'borrow vs own data' idea only asymptotically/heuristically and not under hierarchical exchangeability. Open = the finite-sample width calculus itself; the risk is that it is a mechanical specialization of Dhillon's formula to HCP's weighted empirical distribution and that the GHCP group (Barber/Dobriban orbit) is next to it. Verdict is based on 44 web/arXiv queries + 6 Semantic Scholar citation lookups; provisional on papers I could not reach (see deviations).

what_remains_open: Not found in any retrieved paper: (1) a closed-form or exact-computation law for E[width] (or the distribution of the threshold quantile) of HCP, GHCP, target-only split/full conformal and Dunn et al.'s pooled/double-conformal sets in terms of K, o (and N_j), alpha, with an explicit between-group/within-group decomposition of the score law (e.g. via a random-effects score model where the HCP weighted empirical distribution reduces to a mixture of group-specific score laws and the threshold is an order statistic of that mixture; the HCP mass at +inf and the target-only 1/(o+1)-type granularity enter as finiteness thresholds in K1 and o); (2) the switching point o*(K, alpha, variance ratio) at which target-only conformal beats borrowing (GHCP only shows this empirically and gives o>=14-style triviality cut-offs); (3) an optimal or risk-minimizing merger/combination rule between global and local information with finite-sample validity (GHCP lists it as a next step; D.4 is a sensitivity table; Duchi et al. resizing is heuristic); (4) a lower-bound/minimax statement for width under hierarchical exchangeability with o target labels (all efficiency theory found is single-group iid or asymptotic: Dhillon et al., Yao-He-Gastpar, Lei et al., Zhang et al.). What is NOT open: the idea that borrowing helps when o is small and hurts when o is large (empirical in GHCP, Duchi et al., Zhang et al., Cluster-CP, federated/personalized CP), the single-group expected-width machinery, and the parametric analogue (random-effects prediction intervals / HTS interval: width depends on K, tau^2, sigma^2 through a t_{K-2} factor).
sharpened_claim_if_any: If pursued: 'Under a hierarchical random-scale score model, the threshold of GHCP/HCP/target-only/Dunn sets is an explicit order statistic of a K- and o-dependent mixture; its expected width E[W] = oracle width * (1 + c1/(K1+1) + c2/(o+1)) + terms controlled by the between-group quantile dispersion, with a crossover o*(K, alpha, rho_between) where target-only becomes narrower; and the minimax-optimal local/global merger weight is lambda* = (within-group information)/(within + between) -- with a finite-sample-valid version via GHCP's donor symmetry.' Differentiator versus the existing work is a lower bound or exact (not simulated) crossover, plus the optimal merger weight with validity; a pure width-formula for HCP would be too thin.
value_assessment: Blunt: as a stand-alone paper this is thin for a top statistics journal (JASA/JRSSB/AoS) and marginal for NeurIPS/ICML. Reasons: (a) it analyses existing procedures rather than proposing one; (b) the technical core is Dhillon et al.'s order-statistic integral applied to the HCP weighted empirical law, plus a Gaussian random-effects calculation that collapses to classical prediction-interval algebra; (c) the result is score-distribution dependent, so a clean distribution-free law is unlikely and Gaussian/sub-Gaussian special cases will look like illustrations; (d) the closest group (GHCP: Mallick/Tchetgen Tchetgen/Dobriban/Lee; HCP: Lee/Barber/Willett) has already flagged efficiency and optimal mergers as next steps, so scoop risk within months is real, and a follow-up from them would subsume a width-only paper. The part with real publishable value is item (3)-(4): a lower bound plus an optimal merger with finite-sample validity, which would be an AISTATS/COLT-style or JRSSB-short contribution. For this project (spatial transcriptomics, clusters = donors, o=4-16 labelled clusters) the claim is better used as a supporting lemma/diagnostic (when to stop borrowing across donors) inside a larger methods paper than as the headline.

verdict_reason: No paper found that allocates one labelling budget between PPI for a cluster-level population mean and calibration of prediction sets for a new cluster, and none that traces a Pareto frontier between the two widths. But each half is occupied and the combination is thin. (i) PPI with partially labelled clusters and label allocation across/within clusters: Broska & Howes 2610.09601 (Oct 2026) give variance formulas by labelling design and state that adding a cost model is the next step. (ii) Cost of calibration labels vs conformal set size: Ilyas et al. ICML 2026 give an online stopping rule for i.i.d. units. (iii) Labels in the target group plus calibration across groups: GHCP (Mallick et al., 2608.15500) and HCP (Lee, Barber, Willett) already combine o target-group labels with K calibration groups, without a cost model. (iv) Compromise allocation between two inferential goals is classical survey sampling (Longford 2006, Molefe & Clark 2015). (v) Csillag et al. 2510.16166 show one calibrated conformal set-predictor can drive PPI. Verdict is 'partly_open' on the strength of about 55 attempted queries (45 returned results; 13 quoted-field arXiv queries returned empty and OpenAlex was not run) over arXiv, Crossref, web search and Semantic Scholar, in conformal, PPI, survey-sampling, multilevel-design and psychometric vocabulary; the last rounds of queries (G-theory, cost-optimal evaluation, cluster PPI + new-cluster interval) produced no new close paper.

what_remains_open: Only the integration, and only at specific levels. (a) Nobody has a cost-aware allocation of (number of labelled clusters G_L, units per labelled cluster, labels in the target cluster o) with BOTH a PPI interval width for a cluster-level mean (design or superpopulation target) AND a hierarchical-conformal set width for a new cluster as the two objectives. Broska-Howes supply the PPI half's variance formulas (without costs), GHCP/HCP supply the set half's coverage and empirical widths (without costs or a closed-form width law), Ilyas et al. supply a cost-vs-set-size tradeoff for i.i.d. units. (b) A closed-form or asymptotic WIDTH law for HCP/GHCP sets as a function of K and o (GHCP gives coverage slack of order 1/K and simulations, not an optimisation-ready width formula) appears unpublished. (c) Whether the tradeoff is real: in the cluster dimension labels are non-rival (labelled donors that feed the PPI rectifier also calibrate HCP, as Csillag et al. show in the i.i.d. case), so I infer the genuine tension is only (1) target-donor labels o versus extra labelled donors, and (2) spread of units across donors (PPI favours it) versus within-donor depth. This inference is mine and untested; if it holds, the 'Pareto frontier' is low-dimensional and largely a corollary of the two known formulas. (d) Validity of using the same labels for rectification and calibration with small G_L (few clusters, skewed contributions) is not addressed in anything found.
sharpened_claim_if_any: For a fixed cost model with per-cluster fixed cost and per-unit cost, derive the (G_L, m, o) allocation that minimises a weighted sum of the cluster-robust PPI interval width (Broska-Howes variance) and the GHCP/HCP prediction-set width, and prove a finite-sample width law for hierarchical conformal sets in (K, o) that makes the frontier explicit; show where sharing labels between rectification and calibration is non-rival, and where reuse breaks validity at G_L between 4 and 16. A claim at this level is not yet in the literature I found; a claim at the level 'one budget serves both, optimise it' is not defensible as new.
value_assessment: Blunt: as stated, not enough for a top statistics journal or NeurIPS/ICML on its own. The headline idea is a combination of three recent papers (Broska-Howes Oct 2026, GHCP Aug 2026, Ilyas ICML 2026) plus textbook compromise allocation (Longford). The 'Pareto frontier' follows mechanically once two width formulas exist, and my inference is that labels are non-rival across the two goals in the cluster dimension, which would make the frontier degenerate except for target-donor labels. Window risk is high: Broska-Howes already name the cost-model extension, and the GHCP authors use the ACS PUMS data this project also uses, so a PPI+HCP merger is an obvious next paper for them. What could carry a paper is (b) and (d): a rigorous finite-sample width/coverage theory for hierarchical conformal sets at few calibration clusters, and a validity analysis of label reuse across PPI and calibration at G_L of 4 to 16. That is a narrower, harder theory contribution that belongs inside the PPI paper as a section, not as a separate JOINT paper. Recommendation: do not pursue JOINT as a standalone direction; fold (b)+(d) into the clustered-PPI paper if the main PPI results survive.

open_problems.problem: Calibrated interval inference for J parallel PPI tasks (genes) whose estimators are NOT independent because all tasks are computed on the same G labelled clusters (donors). Stated gaps in the multi-task PPI/empirical-Bayes line: (i) Empirical Bayes rebiasing models per-task bias as exchangeable draws from an unknown law, treats estimators as exactly normal with known second moments and does not propagate CLT error or plug-in error in the variances; (ii) the authors flag that bias exchangeability can fail; (iii) PAS needs average-coverage intervals centred at the shrinkage estimator; (iv) cross-task recalibration PPI is to be combined with shrinkage 'as future work'. None treats tasks that share clusters, so cross-task dependence has rank at most G-1 and G is 4-16. Precise question: with J=50-343 genes and G labelled donors, what interval (t-type finite-G reference, NPMLE bias prior learned across genes, joint covariance across genes) attains average coverage across genes, and when does bias exchangeability across genes hold for a shared-embedding predictor?

open_problems.problem: Prediction sets for a new spot (or new cell) of a new donor when the spots of a donor are spatially dependent, hence not exchangeable, and when the outcome is a vector (many genes). HCP, GHCP and the hierarchical conformal selection methods all assume that observations within a group are exchangeable or i.i.d. given the group law. Stated open directions are more complex within-group structure (time series, vectors of multiple outcomes) and group-feature-conditional guarantees. Precise question: what block-exchangeable or spatial-subsampling version of HCP/GHCP has finite-sample or asymptotic coverage for a new spot in an unseen donor, how much does naive HCP under-cover on real tissue, and how are simultaneous sets over J genes built without paying a J-fold Bonferroni price?

verdict_reason: The generic mechanism in the claim, limma-style empirical-Bayes variance moderation applied to the influence-function variance of an asymptotically linear estimator across many outcomes with few samples (inflated df d0+dg, a few clusters handled by a 'minor modification'), is published: Hejazi, Boileau, van der Laan & Hubbard (arXiv:1710.05451, v4 2022). PPI/PPI++ estimators are asymptotically linear with cluster-level influence values, so the claim is an instance of that recipe. EB across many PPI tasks is also published (Li & Ignatiadis ICML 2025; Lin, Bickel & Ding 2026; Emmenegger et al. 2026), but those pool means, biases or the proxy-label map; they take variances as estimated accurately. I found no paper that applies moderated variances, or df augmentation, to PPI rectifier variances, and none that combines it with few labelled clusters. what_remains_open: Open only at the level of a PPI-specific instantiation, not the idea: (1) Which variance gets moderated. Under PPI++ with all clusters carrying predictions, only the rectifier part rests on n_L-1 (or n_L-2) df, while the prediction-mean part uses all G clusters. The plain limma formula therefore does not transfer: one must moderate the rectifier variance and the rectifier-prediction covariance, and combine them with an unmoderated term. (2) Data-dependent lambda_j: lambda_j is estimated from the same n_L clusters, so the 'exact under normal / scaled-inverse-chi2' statement fails for tuned estimators; I found no treatment of this. (3) Non-Gaussian cluster contributions with skewed clusters: the project's own finding that the reference distribution, not the variance, is wrong means that moderation fixes noisy variances but not heavy tails; Hejazi et al. themselves switched to a logistic reference for this reason, and Ignatiadis & Roquain give a limma-model-free FDR route. (4) Validity under strongly correlated genes (ST genes are highly correlated across clusters), which limma only handles heuristically. (5) Cross-outcome shrinkage of lambda_j or of the rectifier covariance (PAS and Emmenegger et al. do not do this per outcome, as far as read). Everything else in the candidate claim (EB variance moderation, d0+dg df, moderated-t FDR with BH, clustered units) is covered by Smyth 2004, Hejazi et al., and Ignatiadis & Roquain.
sharpened_claim_if_any: For PPI/PPI++ across many outcomes with G_L<=16 labelled clusters, moderate only the rectifier (label-prediction residual) variance and covariance blocks with a limma prior, and prove finite-sample or sign-flip (group-invariance) validity for the tuned estimator, covering data-dependent lambda_j and skewed cluster contributions. The theory for the tuned estimator, not the moderation, is the contribution.
value_assessment: As stated, this does not support a methods paper at a top statistics journal or NeurIPS/ICML/AISTATS: it is a transplant of limma (Smyth 2004) through a recipe already published for influence-function estimators (Hejazi et al.), with a PPI plug-in that two or three lines of notation specify. A referee who knows genomics will see it at once, and Ignatiadis-Roquain (Sep 2026) already covers the FDR-with-moderated-t angle. It could be one component (a section or an add-on arm) of the larger few-cluster paper, with value only if the sharpened version yields a proof for tuned estimators, which is not trivial (item 2) and could be of modest standalone interest. A practical caution from your own results: on the Visium kidney tasks the foundation-model predictors add almost nothing, so the PPI rectifier variance there is close to the plain label variance, and moderation would be moderating essentially label-only intervals; the gain is only meaningful on lung/census-type tasks where predictors help.

verdict_reason: The 'optimal combination of several predictors' half is taken in the PPI literature: Mixture-of-Experts PPI (Gu-Kong-Xia 2026), Multi-Source PPI (Li-Jiang-Zhang 2026), MultiPPI (Cowen-Breen et al. 2026), AM-PPI (2026) and SADA (Shan et al. 2025) all estimate combination weights over several predictors on the labelled data, with best-expert or never-worse-than-labelled-only guarantees; all use i.i.d. units and none handles clusters or a few-cluster reference distribution. The 'post-selection-valid over a finite menu' half is touched only by Shirota (arXiv 2608.10356, unpublished), who shows same-label selection from a fixed finite library is asymptotically harmless when candidate influence functions coalesce and explicitly disclaims finite-sample and unrestricted-tuning claims. Direct analogues exist in conformal prediction (Liang-Zhu-Barber 2024; Hegazy et al. 2025; Zrnic-Jordan stability), so the template is known. I found no paper giving selection-valid or simultaneous PPI intervals over a menu of genuinely different predictors with 4-16 labelled clusters; but the available constructions (cluster-level cross-fitted selection, Bonferroni/max-t over the menu, stability correction) are routine transplants, so the open remainder is thin. About 80 logged queries/lookups (arXiv, Crossref, OpenAlex, web); forward-citation scan of the anchors is provisional because the anchors are too new to have citations.

what_remains_open: Narrowly: (a) selection-valid or simultaneous intervals for PPI/difference/GREG estimators over a finite menu of genuinely different predictors (influence functions that do NOT coalesce) when the number of labelled clusters G is 4-16 and the reference distribution, not only the variance, is wrong (skewed cluster contributions). No retrieved paper treats this: Shirota's finite-library result is asymptotic and needs coalescing influence functions, the multi-predictor PPI papers estimate weights on the same labels with i.i.d. theory, and the conformal selection papers involve neither PPI nor clusters. (b) Few-cluster degrees-of-freedom accounting for K-predictor combination weights: the cluster-level covariance of K predictor residuals is estimated from only G-1 degrees of freedom, so weights are unstable when K is comparable to G; MultiPPI's shrinkage covariance handles the i.i.d. analogue, not the cluster analogue with a small-G reference distribution. (c) Label-free selection criteria (choosing the predictor from unlabelled-cluster predictions alone) with a coverage guarantee: no PPI paper found. All three are open at the level of a precise theorem under a design-based cluster-sampling model, but each is a modest extension of known tools (Bell-McCaffrey/CR2, cluster-level cross-fitting, Zrnic-Jordan stability, simultaneous intervals).
sharpened_claim_if_any: For cluster-sampled (design-based) difference/GREG estimators with 4-16 labelled clusters and a menu of K genuinely different predictors, quantify and fix the coverage loss from choosing the predictor or the combination weights on the same clusters, with finite-G guarantees: cluster-level cross-fitted selection or a stability-corrected interval, plus a small-G reference distribution. It must be shown to matter empirically (K predictors with materially different cluster-level residual variances); on the Visium tasks, where foundation models add almost nothing over a constant predictor, the selection effect is likely negligible, so the claim has bite mainly on the lung and census tasks.
value_assessment: Blunt: as a stand-alone methods paper at a top statistics journal or NeurIPS/ICML/AISTATS, no. The combination half is crowded (five 2025-26 PPI papers); the selection half has direct conformal templates and a general stability theory; the proposed fixes (cluster-level sample splitting, Bonferroni/max-t over K, stability correction) are routine; the only new ingredient would be a finite-G theorem, a small extension of the CR2 / small-cluster literature already treated as prior art. The empirical premise is also weak: the project's own results show the pathology foundation models barely beat a constant predictor on Visium slope estimands, so winner's-curse bias from picking among them is small where it matters least. Defensible uses: a section or ablation inside a larger few-cluster PPI paper (coverage of picking the best of K on the same clusters versus a cross-fitted pick, on lung Xenium and PUMS where predictors differ), or a short note if simulation shows large undercoverage at G<=8 and K>=3. I would not build a paper around it.

verdict_reason: Every ingredient of the claim has a published or preprint owner. (1) PPI/AIPW for U-statistic (pairwise-kernel) estimands where a pair needs both members labelled, with the correction summed over labelled tuples weighted by inverse inclusion probability, a plug-in over all predicted pairs, and a variance-optimal labelling rule: Wang-Huo-Peng-Zou, arXiv:2605.11638 (May 2026); also Kim-Wasserman-Balakrishnan-Neykov (semi-supervised U-statistics, 2024) and Xu-Witten-Shojaie (2025). (2) Design-based unbiased (Horvitz-Thompson) estimation of neighbour-graph edge totals such as the Dirichlet energy (the numerator of Moran/Geary-type statistics) from sampled nodes under general network designs, with joint-inclusion variance: Ajorlou-Mateos-Ruiz (arXiv:2512.17084), going back to Frank/Kolaczyk-style network sampling; also Klusowski-Wu motif counts. (3) Design-based and dependence-robust PPI for spatial data with a block-balance vs SRS comparison and anticipated-variance-optimal allocation via a semivariogram: Shirota (arXiv:2608.10356), plus Salerno-Wu-McCormick (spatial HAC PPI under clustered/soft-block sampling) and Broska-Howes (cluster-robust PPI). (4) The 'scattered vs clustered pairs' trade-off for pair-based spatial statistics is textbook geostatistics for the variogram (Lark 2002; Zimmerman 2006; Marchant-Lark 2007; Mueller-Zimmerman 1999) and point-process window sampling (translation edge correction = inverse pair inclusion probability). Applying the Cassel-Sarndal-Wretman generalized difference estimator to the induced edge population (y_e = h(y_i,y_j), auxiliary h(yhat_i,yhat_j) known for every edge, edge inclusion = both endpoints labelled) is a routine corollary of survey theory. I found no paper that combines PPI/difference estimation with a neighbour-graph estimand under block labelling designs, and no ST paper doing valid inference for Moran's I or ligand-receptor neighbour statistics from histology predictions; that combination is the only open space, and it is thin.

proposals.title: Finite-pool, anytime-valid prediction-powered decisions on donor cohorts: exhaustion-exact e-processes with a known prediction control variate, shared stopping across genes, and a price-of-validity law under skew
proposals.core_claim: Treat the N donors with free predictions as a finite population and the parameter as the cohort (census) gene-wise mean or contrast. Label donors sequentially without replacement, with the next donor chosen from predictions. Use a betting e-process on the control-variate-adjusted donor values Z_i = y_i - lambda_i(f_i - fbar_N), where fbar_N is known exactly because every donor is predicted. This gives finite-sample (not asymptotic) valid confidence sequences and e-values at n_L = 4-16, for any stopping rule, with width -> 0 when n_L = N. Genes share the same donors and stopping time, so e-BH across G genes controls FDR at the stopping time under arbitrary dependence (including the depth factor). The new content would be (i) a width law that separates the prediction gain, which depends on the finite-pool correlation, from the price of finite-sample validity under skew 1-2, and (ii) a rule for which gene panel to stop on.
proposals.theorem_sketch: Setup: fixed pool (y_i, f_i), i=1..N, with y_i in [0,B], f_i in [0,B]; the order of labelling is random, or predictable with known inclusion probabilities. Define Z_t = y_t - lambda_t (f_t - fbar_N) with lambda_t predictable. Let M_t(m) = prod_{s<=t} (1 + nu_s (Z_s - m_s^-)), where m_s^- is the conditional mean of the not-yet-sampled Z's given the past (the WSR20 WoR construction), and nu_s is a predictable bet. Claim A (validity): M_t(theta_N) is a nonnegative supermartingale, so by Ville P(exists t: theta_N not in CS_t) <= alpha, exactly, for every N and every skewed bounded population; the CS has width 0 at t=N. Claim B (width): for the plug-in/Kelly bet, width_t = (1+o(1)) * sigma_Z,N * sqrt(2 log(1/alpha) (1 - t/N)/t), where sigma_Z,N^2 = (1-rho_N^2) sigma_y,N^2 is the finite-pool residual variance at the oracle lambda. This is a Brownian-bridge (not Brownian-motion) correction, and it applies to the control-variate version. Claim C (price of validity): a lower bound showing that, over bounded populations with prescribed skewness, any WoR-valid CS must pay a factor of at least c*sqrt(log(1/alpha)) over the CLT/t width as t/N -> 0, so that at skew ~2 and t=8 the prediction gain (1-rho^2)^{1/2} = 0.74-0.84 (lung) or ~0.95-1 (Visium) is smaller than the price. This would give a decision rule for when predictions are worth using and when to spend labels instead. Claim D (multi-gene): with e-processes E_g,t, e-BH applied at any stopping time tau that is a stopping time of the joint filtration controls FDR <= alpha * G0/G; if the e-processes share the donor factor, the joint-stop rule 'stop when R_t >= r' is admissible with no correction. Key step for A: the Doob martingale of the sample mean under WoR (as in WSR20 and the GE-betting WoR appendix) combined with the fact that fbar_N is deterministic given the pool, so the control variate does not disturb the conditional-mean calculation. Claims B-C are the non-trivial parts and are not yet proved.
proposals.closest_prior_work: (1) Waudby-Smith & Ramdas, 'Estimating means of bounded random variables by betting' (JRSSB 2024), Sec. 5 WoR betting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.09686, and 'Confidence sequences for sampling without replacement' (NeurIPS 2020) https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04347: give WoR betting CS, but not with a prediction control variate or cluster-level structure. (2) Hsu & Shekhar, 'Efficient Sequential Evaluation of LLMs', https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17409: finite question pool, adaptive querying, predictions learned from history, CS by RIPr/betting; closest in mechanism, but unit-level binary correctness and not census-vs-superpopulation, and no multi-outcome e-BH. (3) Kilian et al., 'Anytime-valid, Bayes-assisted PPI' (NeurIPS 2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18000: asymptotic CS, i.i.d. unlabeled stream, not finite pool. (4) Ham, Bojinov, Lindon, Tingley, 'Design-based confidence sequences', https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.08639: design-based CS with covariate adjustment; same philosophy (finite units fixed, randomness from the design). (5) Gaussian-efficient betting under WoR, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.21694: sharpens the bridge correction (Claim B overlaps). (6) Zrnic & Candes, Active Statistical Inference, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03208; Lee & Kim, 'Statistical Optimality of PPI' (SRSWOR), https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08730. (7) Prediction-Powered E-Values, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04294; Active multiple testing with proxy p/e-values, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.05715. Differences: cluster-level (donors), finite-pool control variate with exactly known fbar_N, skew-indexed price-of-validity bound, and joint stopping across genes. All components exist separately.

proposals.title: Conformal selection of atypical donors with only 4-16 labelled calibration clusters: a feasibility frontier and an e-value (randomised) selection rule that removes the 1/(n+1) granularity floor
proposals.core_claim: Deciding which unlabelled donors are atypical (label above a threshold, or large prediction-label discrepancy such as the depth factor) by conformal selection needs conformal p-values built on n_cal = n_L labelled donors. The smallest attainable p-value is 1/(n_L+1), so BH over m test donors makes zero discoveries unless m*alpha_target is compatible with that floor. Claim: an exact feasibility frontier m_max(n_L, alpha), and a randomised, cluster-level conformal e-value (using the within-donor spots as extra exchangeable replicates of the score) that attains non-trivial power with the same finite-sample FDR guarantee.
proposals.theorem_sketch: Let T_j be conformal scores, p_j = (1 + #{i in cal: T_i >= T_j})/(n+1). Proposition 1 (floor): BH at level q over m tests rejects only if some p_(k) <= kq/m; with p >= 1/(n+1), power is identically 0 whenever m < ... i.e. n+1 < m/(q m)... (for k=1: n+1 > m/q), and more generally rejection count R <= floor(q(n+1)) when all test statistics exceed all calibration statistics. So at n_L = 8, q = 0.1, R <= 0 even for perfect scores. Proposition 2 (remedy): replace p_j by a randomised/stochastically-rounded e-value e_j = (n+1) 1{p_j <= c} / ... built from donor-level scores that use within-donor spot replicates, so that E_null[e_j] <= 1 and e-BH has FDR <= q; show the achievable rejection set is not capped by q(n+1). Key step: exchangeability of donors is the only assumption; spots enter only through a donor-level score, so no new assumption. The risk is that Proposition 1 is elementary and Prop. 2 reduces to existing randomised-e-BH (Ramdas-Manole).
proposals.closest_prior_work: Jin & Candes, 'Selection by prediction with conformal p-values', JMLR 2023, https://jmlr.org/papers/volume24/22-1176/22-1176.pdf; Bates et al., 'Testing for outliers with conformal p-values', https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08279 (smaller calibration set -> more conservative/variable FPR); Bashari et al., derandomized conformal e-values https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.07294 (notes 1/(n_cal+1) floor on p-values and effect on p-to-e power); Ramdas & Manole, 'More powerful multiple testing under dependence via randomization', https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11126; Lee & Ren 2025 hierarchical conformal selection (already excluded); Conformal Labeling https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.14581; Active multiple testing with proxy p/e-values https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.05715.

proposals.title: Cheap-assay sufficiency as a sequential decision problem: anytime-valid certificate that using predictions instead of labels changes cohort-level gene decisions by at most epsilon, with a donor-level learning-curve stopping rule for the label split between training and rectification
proposals.core_claim: Replace the interval goal by a go/no-go: after labelling donors one at a time, certify (e-process) H1: the decision d_g(pred-based) differs from d_g(label-based) for at most an epsilon fraction of genes, in the cohort. In parallel, choose the number of labelled donors used to train the head versus rectify using an extrapolated learning curve R^2_c(n_train), because in real use only labelled donors can train the head (the current HEST predictions use ~23 training donors and therefore overstate quality).
proposals.theorem_sketch: Per gene g, let L_g,t in [0,1] be the 0/1 (or bounded margin-based) disagreement loss for donor t's decision contribution; D_t = (1/G) sum_g L_g,t is a bounded donor-level loss. Test H0: pool-mean(D) >= eps by a WoR betting e-process over donors (as in Cand. 1); the gene-level correlation induced by the shared depth factor does not matter because the unit is the donor. Second result: for the cross-fitted difference estimator with n_train + n_rect = n_L donors and R^2_c(n) = R_inf^2 (1 - c/n^beta), the finite-pool variance is V(n_train) proportional to [1 - R^2_c(n_train)(1 - n_rect/N)]/n_rect; the optimum satisfies a first-order condition in n_train/n_L with a closed form for beta=1, showing the optimum is 0 (all donors rectify) when R_inf^2 < 2c/n_L-type threshold, which happens in the Visium regime (R_c^2 ~ 0.05-0.13). Key difficulty: bounded-loss e-process validity is easy; the novelty would be the closed-form threshold under a learning-curve model and an empirical check.
proposals.closest_prior_work: Meta-analytic surrogate-endpoint validation (Buyse/Burzykowski; trial-level R^2 and surrogate threshold effect), e.g. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11609000/ and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.08443: the classical 'few clusters (trials), predict effect from surrogate' framework; Ji, Lei, Zrnic 'Predictions as surrogates', https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.09731 (cited in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.29249); 'Fine-Tune, Then Rectify', https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.19486 (optimal allocation of labels between fine-tuning and PPI); Zrnic & Candes cross-prediction PNAS https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2322083121; Lee & Kim https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08730 (label reuse/variance correction); learning-curve-based sample-size prediction in genomics (Mukherjee et al. 2003; not retrieved, from memory, treat as unverified); Hsu & Shekhar https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17409 for the e-process mechanics.
proposals.data_test: Refit the ridge head on subsets of n_train in {2,4,8,12} labelled donors (CCRCC, Indiana, lung) and trace R^2_c(n_train), within-donor r and decision-agreement with the full-cohort label-based gene decisions; fit the power-law learning curve; compare predicted optimum n_train* with an empirical grid of PPI variance; apply the bounded-loss e-process to the gene-decision disagreement. Also compute the same on ACS (state-level, train head on n states).
proposals.why_a_referee_might_call_it_known: The allocation question is the subject of 'Fine-Tune, Then Rectify' and cross-prediction; exactly unbiased split-sample regression estimators are on the project's prior-art list; the decision-agreement certificate is a standard bounded-loss sequential test, and surrogate validation (STE, trial-level R^2) already treats few-cluster decisions from cheap endpoints.

proposals.title: Non-concentration of multi-gene coverage under a pervasive donor factor: factor-aware false-coverage-proportion (FCP) exceedance intervals for few-donor PPI
proposals.core_claim: With n_L labelled donors and G genes that share one donor-level factor, the number of genes whose interval misses is not binomial. As G grows with n_L fixed, the false-coverage proportion converges to a random variable set by the realised factor sample, so per-gene 95% coverage says almost nothing about how many of the G intervals fail in a given study. A procedure that controls P(FCP > gamma) <= delta, with the dependence estimated from the labelled donors themselves, gives the guarantee a user reading 343 intervals needs. The 'many genes' do not act as replicates.
proposals.theorem_sketch: Setup: donor-level rectifier means r_gc = alpha_g + lambda_g a_c + e_gc (c = 1..n_L, sampled iid or SRS-without-replacement from N donors), a_c mean 0, var 1 (possibly skewed), e idiosyncratic and weakly dependent across genes with variances psi_g. CI_g is the cluster t- (or CR2) interval at level 1-alpha; M_g = 1{CI_g misses}. (i) Non-concentration. Fix n = n_L. If G^{-1} sum_g lambda_g^2/(lambda_g^2+psi_g) -> pi_bar > 0, then FCP_G = G^{-1} sum_g M_g -> h_n(a_1..a_n) in probability, where h_n(a) = lim G^{-1} sum_g P(|T_g| > c | a). Var(h_n) = Cov(M_g, M_g') > 0 is an explicit function of (pi_bar, n, alpha, law of a): for Gaussian a it is a bivariate-t tail probability, and for pi_bar -> 1 it equals alpha(1-alpha). Key step: conditional independence of the idiosyncratic parts given the factor path, a LLN across genes, and a delta-method for studentisation. (ii) Exceedance calibration. In the pure-factor limit, P(FCP > gamma) -> P(|t_{n-1}| > c) for every gamma < 1. Hence a level-alpha t-interval gives P(FCP > gamma) ~ alpha, not P(FCP > gamma) ~ 0, and the critical value needed for P(FCP > gamma) <= delta is the delta-level one, with an interpolating formula for pi_bar < 1. Skewness of a enters through the Edgeworth term of the one scalar studentised factor-sample mean, so it is the same under- or over-coverage for all genes at once. (iii) Estimable bound. Factor loadings and psi_g are consistent as G -> infinity with n fixed (rank-1 plus diagonal, estimated from the labelled donors). The plug-in estimate of h_n at the observed data gives an FCP upper confidence bound whose coverage error -> 0 as G -> infinity, up to the single-scalar studentisation error. A sign-flip/randomisation version has exact finite-n validity for the factor component under symmetry. Non-trivial content: the G -> infinity, n fixed regime, the explicit dispersion index rho_M, the exceedance critical value and the data-driven bound. The ingredients are standard.
proposals.closest_prior_work: Closest in structure is FDP estimation and exceedance control under factor-structured dependence for TESTING: Fan, Han & Gu JASA 2012 and Friguet, Kloareg & Causeur JASA 2009 (both cited in arXiv:1812.08965 and arXiv:1812.07488, only seen as references); FarmTest arXiv:1711.05386; Wang, Zhao, Hastie & Owen 2017 AoS https://doi.org/10.1214/16-AOS1511; permutation FDP bounds arXiv:1808.05528. For COVERAGE: Benjamini-Yekutieli FCR, with an independence-based improvement at https://doi.org/10.1093/jrsssb/qkaf024, and rank-conditional coverage arXiv:1702.06986. Efron's correlated-null work (cited in arXiv:1812.08965) is the other relevant item. Also arXiv:2607.12208 (BH can fail under a factor model; conditional on one latent factor the limiting CDF is random, the same mechanism). I found no paper on FCP exceedance for intervals with few clusters, and none that links it to PPI or cluster-robust PPI (Broska & Howes arXiv:2610.09601 is background). The difference is the estimand: coverage proportion, n_L fixed, G -> infinity, studentised cluster intervals with skew. The mathematical mechanism is the same as the FDP-under-factor literature, so a referee will read it as a translation.
proposals.data_test: Done as a provisional check, finite-population draws from the donors: results/round4/ppi/Q5_joint/q5_cluster_residuals_long.csv.gz, donor x gene mean residuals, 3 encoders. Truth is the all-donor mean, t-interval with fpc, 2000 draws of n_L donors. On CCRCC (24 donors, 50 genes, PC1 share of the rectifier matrix 0.65-0.67, mean gene-gene correlation ~0.61), n_L = 8: SD of the per-draw FCP is 0.108-0.145 vs 0.037-0.043 under a binomial, P(FCP > 0.2) = 0.12-0.18, 95th percentile of FCP 0.30-0.42. Marginal miss rate is only 0.076-0.10. Indiana (PC1 0.30-0.35): SD 0.079-0.097 vs ~0.038. Lung Xenium (343 genes, PC1 0.35-0.47): SD 0.051-0.072 vs 0.012, i.e. up to ~6x. Artifacts: factor_fcp_dispersion_check.csv. Next: (a) implement the plug-in FCP bound and check P(FCP > gamma) <= delta over the same draws; (b) confirm on ACS with PUMA clusters x several income-type outcomes; (c) check that the dispersion index predicted from pi_bar matches the observed one.
proposals.why_a_referee_might_call_it_known: (1) 'This is Fan-Han-Gu/FarmTest FDP under factor dependence with the word coverage substituted.' The duality between intervals and tests makes that a fair reading. The defence is the regime (n_L fixed, so the factor sample itself is a t-distributed scalar, with skew) and the interval-level guarantee, which that literature does not state. (2) 'Simultaneous or FCR-adjusted intervals already control this': Bonferroni does, but at the cost of sqrt(2 log G) widening, which the factor structure shows is unnecessary. The paper's value is that the right price is a single-scalar critical value. (3) The Gaussian bivariate-orthant step is textbook.

proposals.title: Predictable-signature PPI: choosing the gene-combination estimand by PPI efficiency, with weights learned on source donors and a high-dimension-low-sample-size transfer theorem
proposals.core_claim: In a many-outcome panel the estimand can be a linear combination (signature, portfolio) w'mu of genes. PPI efficiency for w'mu is governed by the generalised Rayleigh quotient rho(w) = w'Sigma_r w / w'Sigma_y w (donor-level rectifier covariance over label covariance), so the 'most predictable signature' is the smallest generalised eigenvector (Lo-MacKinlay's maximally predictable portfolio). With n_L < G donors the in-sample minimiser is degenerate (rho_hat -> 0), so the weights must come from donors outside the target labelled set. The paper would give the exact limit of the out-of-donor-sample efficiency and a protocol, with weights from the predictor's own training donors (OOF residuals), whose PPI interval is valid for any pre-specified w and whose realised efficiency is characterised. Under a rank-1 factor, the factor direction is where the predictor is blind and rho ~ 1 - rho_f^2, so the useful contrasts are the factor-orthogonal ones.
proposals.theorem_sketch: Let Sigma_y, Sigma_r be population donor-level covariances and rho* = lambda_min(Sigma_y^{-1} Sigma_r) over the allowed set W. Estimate them from M source donors, G/M -> gamma. (i) Validity: if w_hat is measurable with respect to source donors independent of the target cohort, the cluster-robust PPI interval for w_hat'mu has asymptotic coverage 1-alpha conditional on w_hat. This is immediate. The expected width ratio is sqrt(rho(w_hat)). (ii) Transfer limit: under a spiked model Sigma_y = Lambda + factor spike (with the spike in the denominator and not in the numerator), the out-of-sample ratio rho(w_hat) converges to a deterministic limit determined by Wachter-type generalised-eigenvalue asymptotics, while the in-sample ratio converges to a strictly smaller limit (0 if M <= G). The gap is explicit in gamma and the spike strength. Ridge or factor-orthogonal constraints w ⊥ lambda_hat give a closed-form rule for the ridge weight attaining the limit's minimum. (iii) Ignoring selection (using the target labelled donors to pick w) gives an anti-conservative interval, with an explicit order of the bias of the variance estimate: Sigma_r-hat has rank <= n_L - 1, so w_hat'Sigma_r-hat w_hat can be exactly 0. Proof ingredients: random-matrix generalised eigenvalues (F-matrix / Wachter law) plus conditioning on w_hat. Only (ii) is non-trivial.
proposals.closest_prior_work: Optimisation step: Lo & MacKinlay 1997, maximally predictable portfolios, with data-snooping control https://web.mit.edu/~alo/www/Papers/lo-mackinlay-97.html; Pinelis & Ruppert, arXiv:2311.01985 (maximal portfolio predictability with ML); Goulet Coulombe arXiv:2306.05568 (maximally machine-learnable portfolios); sparse CCA of genes with image features (Nature Commun. 2021, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-21727-x). On the PPI side, MoE-PPI arXiv:2604.27892 chooses the mixture of PREDICTORS minimising the PPI variance and AM-PPI arXiv:2605.08429 allocates among predictors; neither chooses a linear combination of OUTCOMES. Multi-task PPI arXiv:2605.29249 treats tasks separately. I did not find a PPI paper that treats the estimand weights as a design variable. The differences are the PPI-specific efficiency criterion, the HDLSS transfer limit, and the factor-orthogonality statement.
proposals.data_test: Needs the donor x gene matrices of labels and out-of-fold predictions, which are not in this repo (the round-3 B1 parquet files are on Longleaf), so I could NOT run it. Plan: CCRCC (24 donors, 50 genes), Indiana (25 donors), Lung Xenium (15 donors, 343 genes, the real HDLSS case). For random splits of donors into source and target halves, learn w_hat on source, report rho(w_hat) on target against rho of single genes and of the PC1 signature, and compare in-sample and out-of-sample ratios with the theoretical limit. The existing diagnostic results/round9/diagnostics/c0_shared_donor_factor.csv gives a cautionary prior: removing PC1 REDUCED the median between-donor R^2 (hoptimus0 0.079 -> 0.065, resnet50 0.049 -> 0.023, uni_v2 0.127 -> 0.062), so on CCRCC the predictors' donor-level signal partly lives in the factor direction and factor-orthogonal signatures may be LESS predictable. This could kill the idea on CCRCC.
proposals.why_a_referee_might_call_it_known: (1) 'Lo-MacKinlay / Box-Tiao canonical analysis / CCA applied to the PPI criterion.' (2) 'Choosing the estimand to be the one the model predicts best is scientifically circular: a signature is not an estimand of interest unless pre-specified.' This is a conceptual objection and probably the main risk. (3) Validity is trivial once w is independent of the target donors, so the contribution reduces to the HDLSS limit, which is random-matrix theory already known for generalised eigenvalues. Honest summary: the optimisation is old, and the PPI-specific piece is thin.

proposals.title: Factor-orthogonal SURE: prediction-powered shrinkage across genes when all tasks share the same few donors
proposals.core_claim: Prediction-powered adaptive shrinkage (PAS) and multi-task PPI assume tasks are independent, so SURE-tuned shrinkage is asymptotically optimal because the compound loss concentrates. With genes measured on the same n_L donors and a common donor factor, the compound loss does not concentrate: on the rectifier matrices its coefficient of variation is 0.5-1.0, against 0.07-0.2 expected under independence. A SURE-tuned weight then optimises an expectation that the realised loss does not follow. The fix: estimate the (nearly known-direction) factor component, apply SURE shrinkage only in the factor-orthogonal complement, where the noise is weakly dependent and concentration holds, and treat the one-dimensional factor component separately with n_L-based inference.
proposals.theorem_sketch: Model: theta_hat_g = theta_g + lambda_g xi + e_g, xi ~ scale-1/sqrt(n_L) one-dimensional shared error, e_g weakly dependent. (i) For any shrinkage class with data-driven weight omega_hat selected by minimising SURE, L_G(omega_hat) - SURE_G(omega_hat) does NOT converge to 0 in probability as G -> infinity with n_L fixed; the difference converges in law to a non-degenerate functional of xi (explicit for the linear James-Stein class). (ii) Let P_perp be the projection orthogonal to lambda. SURE computed on P_perp theta_hat satisfies the usual uniform concentration, so the P_perp-restricted PAS rule is asymptotically optimal among componentwise-linear shrinkers in the complement; the lambda-component has irreducible risk lambda'lambda * Var(xi) that no cross-gene borrowing can reduce. (iii) Combined risk = optimal-complement risk + irreducible factor risk, and the gain over unrestricted PAS is explicit. Key step: decomposition of the loss into a sum over G-1 weakly dependent coordinates plus a single scalar term.
proposals.closest_prior_work: Prediction-Powered Adaptive Shrinkage Estimation, Li & Ignatiadis, arXiv:2502.14166 (SURE-tuned shrinkage across independent problems, asymptotic optimality). Prediction-Powered Inference Across Many Tasks, arXiv:2605.29249 (shared-structure recalibration; shows affine cross-task recalibration adds nothing asymptotically). Empirical Bayes under correlated noise: Sun & Stephens, arXiv:1812.07488 (factor-model decorrelation, RUV controls). SURE with known covariance: arXiv:2606.12324. The EB-with-correlated-noise literature is close to the whole technical content, so this is the weakest of the three.
proposals.data_test: Done as a provisional check on results/round4/ppi/Q5_joint/q5_cluster_residuals_long.csv.gz (hoptimus0 arm): compound standardised squared error of the n_L-donor mean, 2000 draws; CV(loss) with real genes vs with each gene's donors redrawn independently: CCRCC n_L=4: 1.01 vs 0.21; n_L=8: 0.71 vs 0.17; Indiana n_L=8: 0.50 vs 0.18; Lung (343 genes) n_L=8: 0.54 vs 0.07. (2) Power may be low: PAS's gain at n_L = 4-8 with 50 genes may be small relative to the irreducible factor component. (3) PAS authors could extend their theorem to dependence in one remark.

proposals.title: Between-donor head: within-donor skill is irrelevant for donor-mean estimands, so train a two-block ridge head whose between-donor block is shrunk toward the within-donor slope (label-free prior geometry)
proposals.core_claim: For estimands that are linear in the label (gene mean over donors), the PPI variance depends on the head only through its donor-level (between) component, because the within-donor part of the prediction averages out inside each donor. A pooled spot-level ridge is dominated by within-donor variation (millions of spots vs 4-16 donor means) and therefore transplants the within slope onto the between direction (Mundlak conflation). This leaves a non-vanishing donor-level excess risk floor ||Pi^{1/2} gamma||^2 (gamma = beta_B - beta_W, Pi = covariance of donor-mean embeddings) that does not shrink with more spots or more labelled donors. Proposed head: within block fitted on spots; between block fitted on the G_L-1 donor means by ridge CENTRED at the within slope, with the prior covariance taken from the donor-mean embedding spectrum of ALL donors (label-free) and tau chosen by nested leave-donor-out on the donor-level PPI criterion. Consequence for the data: donor R^2_c (0.05-0.13 on CCRCC) versus within r (~0.16-0.20) is a diagnostic of gamma.
proposals.theorem_sketch: Setup: donors g=1..G exchangeable, spots i=1..m_g, x_gi = mu_g + z_gi (E z=0), E[y_gi | x] = beta_W'z_gi + beta_B'mu_g + u_g, Pi = Cov(mu), Sigma_z = within covariance, estimand theta = E[ybar_g]. Cross-fit (leave-one-labelled-donor-out) linear head h(x)=a + b'x. (i) Identity: with m_g -> infinity, the PPI estimator theta_hat = (1/G) sum_g fbar(xbar_g) + (1/n_L) sum_l (ybar_l - f^{(-l)}(xbar_l)) has asymptotic variance (1/n_L) Var(ybar - b_{-l}' xbar) + O(1/G): it depends on the head only through b applied to donor means; any head component orthogonal to the span of Pi is irrelevant. (ii) Pooled-ridge limit: the pooled ridge solution satisfies b_pool = (S_W + S_B + lam I)^{-1}(S_W beta_W + S_B beta_B) with S_W ~ N_spots*Sigma_z and S_B ~ G_L*Pi; as m -> infinity with G_L fixed, b_pool -> beta_W on range(Sigma_z), so the donor-level excess risk converges to E||Pi^{1/2}(beta_B-beta_W)||^2_{range(Sigma_z)} > 0 (an irreducible floor in the learning curve in BOTH m and G_L). (iii) Two-block head: with b_B ~ ridge toward beta_W-hat with prior covariance tau^2 Pi, excess donor-level risk <= min{ ||Pi^{1/2}gamma||^2 (+ O(1/N_spots)), sigma_u^2 d_eff(tau)/G_L + (shrinkage bias) } with d_eff(tau) = tr[Pi (Pi + (sigma_u^2/(G_L tau^2)) I)^{-1}], giving a data-adaptive interpolation between 'transplant the within slope' (tau=0) and pure donor-level ridge (tau=inf); d_eff is computable from the label-free donor-mean spectrum of all donors. (iv) Hence the PPI width ratio satisfies ratio^2 -> 1 - R_B^2 (donor-level), and an oracle inequality for tau selected by nested leave-donor-out. Key proof steps: Frisch-Waugh block decomposition of the normal equations; a deterministic-equivalent / effective-dimension bound for ridge with informative centre (standard once the donor-level problem is reduced to G_L points in R^p). Non-trivial part to prove: validity of the nested-LODO choice of tau at G_L=4-16 (finite-G oracle inequality, not asymptotics). Not verified by me: only the algebra of (i)-(ii) is a sketch; I did not run it on real data.

(f) Mozer, PPI = difference estimator (PPI++ = GREG): https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19160 .
