Difference: none of these retrieved papers trains a frozen-embedding head for clustered PPI by splitting within/between blocks, uses the within slope as the prior centre of the donor-level ridge, or derives the irreducible pooled-head floor in the p >> G_L regime.
proposals.data_test: Per-donor mean embeddings (results/round4/ppi/Q5_joint/q5_mean_embeddings__*.parquet) and leave-donor-out residual tables already exist; spot-level embeddings/labels are needed for beta_W (on the cluster). For CCRCC (24), Indiana (25), lung Xenium (15): resample labelled sets of size G_L in {4,8,12} (finite-population truth = mean over all donors) and compare, per gene and encoder: constant head, current pooled ridge, within slope transplanted to donor means, two-block head with nested-LODO tau. Metrics: donor-level R^2_c, width ratio vs labelled-only, coverage of t_{G-1} and CR2-type intervals. Predictions: largest gain on lung Xenium (within r ~0.62 vs R^2_c ~0.24, i.e. large estimated gamma defect); little on CA PUMAs (R^2_c 0.95) and on Visium kidney where donor means are dominated by the depth factor. ACS: states as clusters, PUMAs/persons as units, within block = within-state slope.
proposals.why_a_referee_might_call_it_known: Mundlak/hybrid models and the observation that cluster-total regression beats individual-level regression are classical in econometrics and survey sampling; 'ridge centred at a prior estimate' is routine; a referee may say the contribution is Mundlak + ridge applied to PPI. The defensible novelty is the finite-G oracle inequality, the irreducible-floor statement for pooled heads, and the label-free effective-dimension d_eff; if those prove straightforward the paper is thin.

proposals.title: Conditional-on-embeddings linear-weights form of leave-donor-out ridge PPI: coverage-error expansion in the effective number of donors, and coverage-aware tuning of encoder and penalty
proposals.core_claim: For a ridge head (a linear smoother) and a mean-type estimand, the leave-donor-out cross-fit PPI estimator is exactly theta_hat = sum_l w_l(X, lambda) * ybar_l with sum_l w_l = 1, where the weights depend only on label-free embeddings of ALL donors, the penalty and the labelled set. Conditional on the embeddings the estimator is a weighted sum of independent donor means, so higher-order theory is classical but the head enters through computable quantities: effective donors n_eff = 1/||w||_2^2, the Lyapunov ratio ||w||_3^3/||w||_2^3, and a conditional calibration defect b(lambda) = sum_l w_l m(xbar_l) - mean_g m(xbar_g). These govern the coverage error of few-donor intervals, so the coverage-optimal (encoder, lambda) differs from the MSE-optimal one, and part of the choice can be made without labels.
proposals.theorem_sketch: Let T = (theta_hat - theta)/se_hat, se_hat^2 = sum_l w_l^2 e_l^2/(1-h_l) (HC2/CR2-type, e_l = LOCO residual, h_l a leverage term computable from w). Conditional on X, donor means are independent with errors eps_l of variance sigma_l^2, third and fourth standardized cumulants kappa_3,l, kappa_4,l. Claim: P(|T| <= z) = 1 - alpha + (1/n_eff) * C(z; kappa, L_3, L_4) + O(n_eff^{-3/2}) + noncentrality term phi-type in b(lambda)/se, where the n_eff^{-1/2} one-sided term cancels for two-sided intervals, L_3 = ||w||_3^3/||w||_2^3 (the n^{-1/2} Lyapunov term), and C collects (kappa_4, kappa_3^2, variance-estimator bias) with the same polynomials as the studentised mean, replacing n by n_eff and kappa by weighted cumulants (Bhattacharya-Rao Thm 20.6 conditional on X, plus Hall-type expansion of the studentiser). Corollary: the width-vs-coverage Pareto set over (encoder, lambda) is computable from {w, residual moments}; a Cornish-Fisher critical value c(n_eff, kappa_3_hat, kappa_4_hat) (cf. Gafarov-Ura for OLS clusters) gives O(n_eff^{-3/2}) coverage error. For small lambda with p > G_L, ||w||_2 inflates (interpolating head) so n_eff collapses: a label-free warning. What I verified (toy simulation only, p=200, G=24, n_L in {4,8,12}, 200 replications, not real data): the estimator is unbiased (bias |.| <= 0.075 vs sd 0.3-0.8), sum_l w_l = 1 to three decimals, and n_eff = 1/sum w^2 ranged 3.0-8.9; the delete-one-labelled-donor Efron-Stein jackknife was conservative by a factor 1.7-3.3 relative to the Monte-Carlo variance, i.e. too crude to use, which motivates the weights-based HC/CR2 studentiser. Not verified: the Edgeworth statement itself.
proposals.closest_prior_work: (a) Shirota, design-based/conditional-validity PPI for spatial data (noncentrality from calibration defect; same-label selection from a finite library): https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10356 . (b) Gafarov & Ura, Refined cluster-robust inference (Cornish-Fisher critical values with score skewness/kurtosis, ~10 clusters; OLS): https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24786 . (c) Calonico-Cattaneo-Farrell, coverage-error-optimal tuning (precedent for choosing the tuning parameter for inference not MSE; local polynomials): https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.01398 . (d) Cross-PPI (iid, asymptotic stability assumption): https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16598 ; Statistical optimality of PPI incl. single-fit variance correction: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08730 ; No Free Lunch (non-asymptotic PPI++, optimistic variance without splitting): https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20178 . (e) Bates-Hastie-Tibshirani, CV standard errors too small and nested CV: https://tibshirani.su.domains/ftp/NCV.pdf ; V-fold jackknife t_{V-1} for fixed V: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22493 . (f) Mozer (PPI = difference estimator): https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19160 ; Prediction-powered conditional inference tuning from unlabeled covariates only: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05575 . Difference: none retrieved gives an Edgeworth/coverage analysis of PPI, the weights representation of leave-cluster-out ridge PPI with p >> G_L, or coverage-aware head selection; but each ingredient has a clear classical analogue.
proposals.data_test: Same resampling design as proposal 1 on CCRCC, Indiana, lung (finite-population truth over all donors, G_L in 4..16, many labelled subsets): (1) compute w for each encoder x lambda grid from mean embeddings alone; (2) report n_eff, L_3 against realised coverage of t_{G-1}, CR2 and Cornish-Fisher intervals, and against the skewness of donor residuals (CCRCC donor means have skewness ~2); (3) compare lambda chosen by LODO MSE with lambda chosen by predicted coverage-adjusted width, using nested LODO to avoid selection optimism. ACS states (51) and CA PUMAs (265) as skew-free controls.
proposals.why_a_referee_might_call_it_known: PPI = GREG (Mozer) and GREG weights are a linear form, so the weights representation is expected; heteroskedasticity-robust studentisation of linear estimators, Cornish-Fisher corrections (Gafarov-Ura) and coverage-error-optimal tuning (Calonico et al.) are existing tools; Shirota already covers conditional noncentrality and same-label selection from a library. The paper would be an assembly of known tools for this setting unless the head-dependent expansion yields a surprising result (e.g. coverage-optimal lambda provably larger than MSE-optimal lambda).

proposals.title: Factor-pooled donor-level head: one regression for the shared technical (depth) factor plus gene-wise residual heads
proposals.core_claim: In CCRCC one donor factor (|corr| 0.998 with average expression) carries 65% of between-donor variance (median gene 73%), and predictions see it only weakly (|corr| 0.32-0.43). Gene-by-gene donor-level heads each re-learn the same factor from 4-16 donors in p >> G_L dimensions. Pooling genes through a rank-one factor reduces the label noise of the donor-level regression by about 1/J (J genes) and gives each gene a shared control variate a_j * F_hat(xbar). The ceiling is explicit: the width ratio is no smaller than sqrt(1 - s_j * R_F^2 - residual-head gain), so with R_F^2 <= ~0.18 (from the measured correlations) the gain on CCRCC is small; it is informative mainly as a bound and for tasks with larger factor predictability.
proposals.theorem_sketch: Model: ybar_gj = a_j F_g + e_gj, F_g = psi'mu_g + eta_g, e_gj independent over genes with variance sigma_e^2. Estimating psi by ridge from the J-gene factor score has noise variance sigma_e^2/J + sigma_eta^2 instead of sigma_e^2 + a_j^2 sigma_eta^2 for a gene-wise head; the leave-donor-out excess risk of F_hat is (d_eff/G_L)(sigma_eta^2 + sigma_e^2/J). For gene j the PPI width ratio is sqrt(1 - rho_j^2) with rho_j^2 = s_j R_F^2 + (1-s_j) R_{e,j}^2, and the pooled head dominates the gene-wise head whenever J exceeds a threshold J*(sigma_e^2, sigma_eta^2, d_eff, G_L). Proof: reduced-rank/ridge risk decomposition at the donor level. Not verified; and the gain is capped by the measured weak factor predictability.
proposals.closest_prior_work: PPI across many tasks (cross-task recalibration, not donor factors): https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29249 ; MultiPPI (multiple predictors, cost allocation): https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.27414 ; mixture-of-experts PPI: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27892 ; reduced-rank regression and multi-outcome factor regression are classical (generic retrieved examples only, e.g. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12261392/ ). Surrogate-variable/RUV-type removal of technical factors in genomics was not searched specifically.
proposals.data_test: Use c0_shared_donor_factor.csv diagnostics and per-donor mean embeddings: regress the donor PC1 score on mean embeddings with nested LODO ridge, and compare donor-level R^2_c per gene for (gene-wise head) vs (factor head + gene residual head) at G_L in 4..16 on CCRCC/Indiana/lung. Report the implied bound sqrt(1 - s_j R_F^2).
proposals.why_a_referee_might_call_it_known: Reduced-rank / supervised-PCA multi-outcome regression and multi-task shrinkage are textbook; multi-task PPI exists; and the data indicate the factor is only weakly predictable from images, so the practical gain is small. The depth factor is also the classical target of normalisation in genomics. I rate it likely taken for the method and low-yield for the data.

proposals.title: Set-covariance (edge-corrected) PPI for point-pattern statistics with free locations and predicted marks, labelled by tissue windows
proposals.core_claim: In Xenium/Visium-HD-type data the cell/nucleus locations are known everywhere from the H&E image (free), and only the marks (cell type, gene-on/off state) are expensive. Colocalisation estimands (cross-K, mark-connection function, neighbourhood-enrichment) are pair statistics of the marks. If a window W of the section is labelled, a pair (i,j) is labelled only if both cells fall in W, so the pair inclusion probability is the set-covariance of the window, pi(h)=gamma_W(h)/|D|, and decays with pair distance r. The claim is (i) an unbiased pairwise-HT rectifier with these weights, (ii) a closed-form variance, (iii) a gain law: the correlation between predicted and true pair indicators is roughly the squared mark accuracy, so PPI helps second-order statistics far less than first-order proportions, and there is a critical r*(W, accuracy) beyond which PPI is worse than labelling-only.
proposals.theorem_sketch: Setup. Cluster g has fixed locations x_1..x_N in D_g (conditioned on, free); marks M_i in {1..K} random; predicted marks Mhat_i free. Estimand theta_g(r)=sum_{i!=j} 1{M_i=a,M_j=b,|x_i-x_j|<=r}/(n_a n_b) (or its pair-count numerator, with n_a,n_b either known from predictions or ratio-linearised). Labelling: translate of a window B placed uniformly at random (or systematic lattice of windows), W=B+U. Pair inclusion pi_ij=P(x_i,x_j in W)=gamma_B(x_i-x_j)/|D_g|-type set-covariance (boundary-adjusted), strictly decreasing in |x_i-x_j|. Estimator: theta_hat = sum_{all pairs} u(Mhat_i,Mhat_j) + sum_{pairs in W} [u(M_i,M_j)-u(Mhat_i,Mhat_j)]/pi_ij. Claim 1 (exact unbiasedness, finite-population/design-based): E_W[theta_hat]=theta_g(r) for every predictor, by pairwise HT. Claim 2 (variance): Var = sum_{(ij),(kl)} (pi_{ij,kl}-pi_ij pi_kl)/(pi_ij pi_kl) Delta_ij Delta_kl with Delta_ij=u-uhat; pi_{ij,kl}=P(four cells in W) is a four-point set-covariance; Hajek projection gives leading term (1/m_eff) Var(sum_j Delta_ij / pi_ij ...) with m_eff=|D|/|B|. Claim 3 (gain law): under a symmetric misclassification model with accuracy p, corr(u,uhat) = O(p^2 - chance), so Var(Delta)/Var(u) ~ 1-rho^2 with rho scaling like the SQUARE of the single-mark rho; and Var grows like 1/gamma_B(r) so that for r comparable to the window diameter the rectifier variance diverges; define r*(B,p) as the crossing point against labelled-only HT. Claim 4 (cross-cluster): with n_L clusters the cluster-level analogue is the usual difference estimator, and the within-cluster window variance is an additive second-stage term (two-stage). Key proof step: pair inclusion via the set-covariance function and a four-point version of Matheron/Ohser edge-correction identities; delta method for the ratio normalisation.
proposals.closest_prior_work: (1) Shirota, 'Design-based PPI for spatial data' / 'Conditional validity of PPI for spatially dependent finite populations', arXiv:2608.10356 - design-based PPI on pixel populations with nonuniform acquisition, regression coefficients (first-order estimating equations), NOT pair/point-pattern statistics. (2) Zou et al., 'Learning U-Statistics with Active Inference', arXiv:2605.11638 - U-statistic PPI/active inference with i.i.d. units, no window geometry. (3) Earlier session verdict (PPI for pairwise spatial U-statistics with block labelling, mostly taken: Wang-Huo-Peng-Zou 2026, Ajorlou et al.) - I could not retrieve Wang-Huo-Peng-Zou itself this session (search returned only 2605.11638 from the same group), so the overlap with it is unverified. (4) Point-process side: Myllymaki et al. deviation tests for marked patterns arXiv:1306.1028 and mark-weighted K-functions; Statistical Analysis of Quantitative Cancer Imaging Data arXiv:2409.08809 (review of cross-K for cell types). None of these uses predicted marks plus a labelled window. Difference: the pair-inclusion = set-covariance structure and the squared-accuracy gain law. 11 web searches and 30 arXiv queries found no paper that does this, but absence in a keyword search is weak evidence.
proposals.data_test: Lung Xenium (14-15 donors, 343 genes): define marks as thresholded expression of a gene (or cluster-derived cell type) at cell/bin level, predicted marks from the UNI/H-optimus-0 + ridge head (leave-donor-out) at the same cells; positions are exact. Estimand: cross-K / mark-connection for gene pairs at r in 20-200 um. Simulate window labelling (random translates of a square window covering 10-40% of the section, plus systematic lattices) on each donor, compare (a) labelled-window-only edge-corrected K, (b) PPI with pairwise HT weights, (c) naive predicted-mark K; report bias, empirical variance vs closed form, coverage, and the crossing r*. Check the squared-accuracy law by regressing pair-indicator correlation on single-mark correlation across genes. ACS PUMS has no spatial point structure, so it is not applicable.
proposals.why_a_referee_might_call_it_known: Pairwise-HT with set-covariance weights is exactly Ripley/Ohser edge correction; PPI for U-statistics and block labelling is claimed by Wang-Huo-Peng-Zou 2026 and Zou et al. 2605.11638; 'second-order statistics need accuracy squared' is the standard attenuation of products of misclassified indicators. The only non-trivial parts are the four-point variance and the r* threshold.

proposals.title: Technical-factor-orthogonalised PPI: estimand invariance to a shared depth/detection factor invisible to the image
proposals.core_claim: One rank-one donor factor (the depth/detection factor: 65% of between-donor variance over 50 CCRCC genes, 73% for the median gene; 31% Indiana; 34% lung) is almost invisible to the image predictor (|corr| 0.32-0.43). Under a simple orthogonal decomposition, the cluster-level R^2 of the predictor on the factor-free part is inflated by 1/(1-s) relative to the raw R^2, and PPI width ratios improve accordingly. The proposal is to define the estimand as the factor-orthogonal part theta_j^perp = E[z_gj - beta_j f_g], estimate f from the labelled clusters' other genes (cross-fitted), and give the PPI interval, its variance, and the cost of estimating f with few labelled clusters.
proposals.theorem_sketch: Model for cluster-mean vectors z_g in R^p: z_g = mu + b f_g + w_g, f_g scalar with Var f = sigma_f^2, w_g independent of f; predictor means P_g = c + gamma b f_g + q_g with gamma small. Let s_j = b_j^2 sigma_f^2 / Var(z_gj). Proposition A: if Cov(w,q) carries all the signal, corr^2(z_j, P_j) = (1-s_j) rho_w^2 + O(gamma), whereas corr^2(z_j^perp, P_j^perp)=rho_w^2, hence R^2 inflation = 1/(1-s_j) (3.7x at s=0.73). Proposition B (width): the PPI++ cluster-level width ratio goes from sqrt(1-(1-s)rho_w^2) to sqrt(1-rho_w^2); with rho_w^2 = R2_raw/(1-s) this is a function of observables. Proposition C (estimation cost): with n_L labelled clusters, f_g and b are estimated by the first principal component of the n_L x p matrix; the estimation error of f_g is O_p(p^{-1/2}) per cluster (many genes), so the plug-in orthogonalised rectifier has the same first-order variance as the oracle as p->infinity with n_L fixed (a large-p, fixed-n_L result, which is the non-standard regime), but the loading estimate b_hat carries O_p(n_L^{-1/2}) error that enters the second-order term; give the Hajek-type correction. Proposition D (validity): the interval covers theta^perp (not theta) at the nominal level whatever the predictor; coverage for raw theta requires E[f]. Key step: Neyman-orthogonality of the PPI estimating equation with respect to (b, f) when f enters linearly, plus fixed-n_L / large-p consistency of PC1 (Bai-Ng / Fan-Liao type, 'blessing of dimensionality').
proposals.closest_prior_work: Removal of unwanted variation with control genes: Gagnon-Bartsch & Speed RUV (arXiv:1211.4259 retrieved as 'Correcting gene expression data when neither unwanted variation nor factor of interest are observed'), Wang-Blei-style unification arXiv:1705.08393 ('Unifying and generalizing methods for removing unwanted variation based on negative controls'); SVA/RUV-III. PPI side: multi-task PPI with cross-task recalibration arXiv:2605.29249 (shares information across tasks, no factor/estimand change); Demystifying PPI arXiv:2601.20819. No search hit combined RUV-style factor removal with PPI estimand definition. The specific retrieved evidence is only that RUV/SVA is standard and that multi-task PPI does not do this.
proposals.data_test: Use the existing 24x50 CCRCC, 25-donor Indiana and 15-donor lung donor x gene matrices. Fit PC1 on labelled donors only, residualise labels and predictions, then run the existing PPI/difference estimator on raw vs orthogonal estimands over n_L in {4,8,12,16} with repeated random labelled sets; report R^2_c, width ratio, coverage (with the t/sign-flip reference already in the project), and the loss from estimating f with n_L donors. Expected: R^2 inflation of about 1/(1-s) if the factor is orthogonal to the predictor, but width ratios move only modestly when raw R^2 is 0.05-0.13 (e.g. 0.97 -> about 0.9); this is a prediction from the algebra, not a computed result.
proposals.why_a_referee_might_call_it_known: Normalising for library size / removing a first PC with control genes is routine RUV/SVA practice, and 'change the estimand' is not a methodological contribution. The only publishable piece would be the fixed-n_L, large-p validity theorem and a clean statement of what estimand the interval covers.

proposals.title: Functional PPI for image-geometry estimands (expression profiles against distance to an image-derived interface) with cluster-level functional control variates and sup-t bands
proposals.core_claim: The H&E image yields a free, exact geometric coordinate for every spot of every cluster (signed distance d to the tumour-stroma or tissue-edge interface). Natural estimands are curves theta(d)=E_g[T_g(d)] where T_g(d)=E[Y|d,g]. Predicted curves P_g(d) exist for all G clusters. A functional difference estimator with a d-dependent tuning lambda(d) plus a sup-t band calibrated by cluster sign-flipping gives uniform (in d) coverage with n_L=4-16 clusters; the gain is a function G(d)=1-rho_g(d)^2 that is typically worst at the interface where tissue is sparse.
proposals.theorem_sketch: Let T_g, P_g in C[d0,d1] be cluster-level curves (local-linear smooths; with thousands of spots per cluster the within-cluster smoothing error is o_p(G^{-1/2}) when n_g h^{3}/log->infinity). SRSWOR of n_L of G clusters. Estimator theta_hat(d)=mean_{all}P_g(d)+lambda(d) mean_{L}(T_g-P_g)(d). Claim 1: sqrt(n_L)(theta_hat-theta) converges in C[d0,d1] to a centred Gaussian process with covariance (1-n_L/G) Cov(T-lambda(T-P)...) (finite-population functional CLT, Hajek-type, following Cardot-Degras-Josserand for model-assisted functional estimators). Claim 2: optimal lambda(d)=Cov(T(d),T(d)-P(d))-type ratio pointwise; the sup-t band c_alpha from the sign-flip distribution of the max-standardised process has exact level 1-2^{1-n_L}-granularity and asymptotic level otherwise; with n_L=4 only 16 sign patterns, so the finest attainable level is 1/8: band construction must be randomised or switch to a t-process (Gaussian-process) reference when n_L<~8. Claim 3: PPI gain is uniform only if lambda(d) varies; a single scalar lambda can lose power at d where rho_g(d) is small (non-monotone). Key step: sup-norm tightness of the cluster-level process plus finite-population CLT; the new content would be the small-n_L granularity result for sup-t sign-flip bands.
proposals.closest_prior_work: Cardot, Degras, Josserand, 'Uniform convergence and asymptotic confidence bands for model-assisted estimators of the mean of sampled functional data', arXiv:1204.6382 (functional model-assisted bands in survey sampling, no PPI, no few-cluster granularity). Simultaneous bands for functional data: Degras arXiv:0908.1980; conformal bands for functional data arXiv:2106.01792, arXiv:1302.6452. PPI side: Shirota arXiv:2608.10356 (spatial design-based PPI, pixel-level), stratified PPI arXiv:2406.04291, multi-task PPI arXiv:2605.29249. Earlier-session verdict on sign-flip few-cluster randomisation for PPI (partly open, thin: Canay-Romano-Shaikh, Ibragimov-Mueller) applies to Claim 2. I found no PPI paper for curve-valued estimands, but a referee would regard it as functional GREG plus PPI++.
proposals.data_test: Kidney (CCRCC/Indiana) and lung: segment tissue by the image (or by predicted tumour probability from an H&E classifier), compute d(s) per spot, build cluster curves of mean log1p expression for the 50-343 genes on a grid of 10-20 distances, run the functional difference estimator against the cluster-mean-only classical estimator for n_L in {4,8,12,16}; report band coverage, band width ratio and the interface-versus-bulk gain G(d). ACS: use distance-to-state-centroid or PUMA rank as a toy coordinate only as a sanity check.
proposals.why_a_referee_might_call_it_known: Functional model-assisted survey estimation with uniform bands (Cardot et al.) plus PPI++ with a d-dependent tuning is a direct composition; the geometry is just a covariate. The sign-flip granularity point is a known property of randomisation tests with few units.

notes: HONEST SUMMARY: under the spatial/image lens nothing I found is clearly open, and I rank the three proposals as one 'uncertain' and two 'likely_taken'. A structural observation explains why: with thousands of spots per labelled cluster, the cluster mean is an almost deterministic functional of the latent field (infill regime), so within-cluster spatial dependence is a second-order term for the whole-cluster labelling regime. The few-cluster reference-distribution problem (skewness ~2.0 on CCRCC donor means) is therefore a purely between-cluster problem and spatial structure gives no handle on it; I tried to derive a random-field (log-Gaussian Cox / multiplicative-depth) skewness for the cluster mean and dropped it because the skew comes from the donor-level depth factor, which neither within-cluster data nor the image predictor sees (this reasoning is analytic, not computed). Spatial dependence only matters in the partial-labelling (window/few-units) regime, which the earlier checkers found mostly taken (Mandallaz-Ye, Shirota, stereology). Double-bootstrap/prepivoting calibration is Beran 1987/Hall. I found NO paper applying this to PPI/GREG-type estimators with predictions known for all clusters under SRS/rejective/cube selection of a handful of labelled clusters, nor a transport-distance bound on coverage error in that setting. The combination is unpublished in what I retrieved, but every ingredient is prior art. Search was incomplete (no OpenAlex, no forward citations), so the 'open' parts are provisional.

what_remains_open: (1) The instantiation: pseudo-population on all G clusters built from predictions known for every cluster, applied to the cluster-level PPI/GREG estimator, design replayed exactly (enumeration for SRS of n_L<=16 of G=14-50, rejection simulation for Mahalanobis-rejective, simulated cube), studentized quantiles replacing t_{n-1}. I found no paper doing this for PPI/GREG with few labelled clusters. (2) A finite-n coverage-error bound via a transport/Kolmogorov distance between true and pseudo standardized-residual laws for fixed small n_L; the survey bootstrap theory I found (Wang-Peng-Kim, Booth-Butler-Hall, Lombardia et al.) is asymptotic/Edgeworth. A finite-population Berry-Esseen literature for sampling without replacement probably exists but I did not retrieve it; check. (3) The second-predictor pseudo-outcome idea (residual shape from a source independent of the labelled clusters): not found, but it is the superpopulation-model bootstrap with an external residual law, so novelty is in application and diagnosis. Key caveat: with residuals taken from only 4-16 labelled clusters the pseudo-population inherits the same few-cluster estimation error as the t reference (pairs bootstrap-t fails at G~6; subject bootstrap underestimates with few subjects). Known-for-all f_g fixes only the regression part, not the residual skewness that drives your under-coverage.
sharpened_claim_if_any: Defensible claim: for the cluster-level PPI/GREG estimator under a known without-replacement or rejective cluster-selection design with fixed small n_L, the design-exact reference distribution of the studentized statistic computed on a pseudo-population whose residual law comes from a source independent of the n_L labelled clusters (second predictor / out-of-sample residuals / pooling across genes) has coverage error bounded by a distance between true and pseudo studentized-residual laws, and beats t_{n_L-1} and the labelled-residual bootstrap in the skewed-contribution regime. Novelty = independent residual source + finite-n bound; the plain labelled-residual pseudo-population is the existing survey bootstrap.
value_assessment: Blunt: as a standalone methods paper for JASA/JRSSB/AoS this is thin. The recipe is the model-based pseudo-population finite-population bootstrap with design replay (Booth-Butler-Hall, Lombardia et al., Wang-Peng-Kim, Cohen-Fogarty) applied to an estimator already known to be the survey difference/GREG estimator; a referee will read it as survey bootstrap-t for the GREG with few PSUs. A finite-n transport-distance bound is the only theorem-level candidate, and its usefulness is limited because the pseudo-population residual law is estimated from the same few clusters that cause the problem. It could support an AISTATS/ICML-level methods-plus-empirics paper, or a section within a larger PPI-for-clustered-spatial-transcriptomics paper, if the independent-residual-source variant restores coverage where t, CR2 and the labelled-residual bootstrap fail on HEST/PUMS and the lineage is cited explicitly. Do not claim the pseudo-population/design-replay idea as new.

verdict_reason: Each ingredient of the claim has a published owner. (1) The selection model itself, arbitrary dependence on observed covariates plus a bounded residual odds ratio, is Sahoo-Lei-Wager's 'conditional Gamma-biased sampling' (arXiv:2209.01754; they note it extends the Aronow-Lee model). (2) Sharp partial-identification intervals for a population mean from a sample with bounded selection odds are Aronow & Lee 2013, Miratrix-Wager-Zubizarreta 2018, and Tudball et al. 2023 (logistic-odds sensitivity parameters, population-level auxiliary constraints, valid CIs). The covariate-conditional sharp bounds follow from Tan's MSM / Dorn-Guo, applied with 'selected' playing the role of 'treated'. (3) MSM bounds for extrapolating across sites/locations with covariate balancing are Nie-Imbens-Wager 2021. (4) A label-free representativeness diagnostic using a covariate/proxy known for the whole population is Tipton's generalizability index (sites/schools, with small-sample (10-70 sites) calibration in Tipton et al. 2017) and Andridge-Little's proxy pattern-mixture analysis / Little et al.'s SMUB, in which the proxy is exactly a fitted prediction of Y known for everyone. (5) Jin-Egami-Rothenhausler (PNAS 2025) already use label-free observed covariate shift across 65 sites to bound the unobserved conditional shift, i.e. a data-driven way to calibrate Gamma. I found no paper that combines these with PPI estimators or with a clustered cohort of 14-50 clusters and 4-16 labelled ones. Demystifying PPI (Song et al. 2026) explicitly flags PPI under MNAR as a failure mode with no sensitivity method, and Broska & Howes (cluster-robust PPI) contain no selection or sensitivity content. So the remaining open piece is the specific combination, which looks like an application of known machinery. This is from 37 distinct queries; arXiv API and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited so coverage rests mostly on web_search and Crossref, and a negative on a combination is weaker evidence than a positive.

value_assessment: Blunt: as stated, no. The sensitivity model (Sahoo-Lei-Wager / Aronow-Lee / Tudball), sharp bounds (Tan, Dorn-Guo), site-level transport bounds (Nie-Imbens-Wager), and the label-free diagnostic (Tipton, Andridge-Little/SMUB, Jin et al.) all exist, so a reviewer at JASA/Biometrika/JRSSB/NeurIPS would read 'plug a PPI predictor into the MSM and apply it to clusters' as an incremental application. The only substantive remainder is valid inference for sharp or conservative bounds with 4-16 clusters; that is hard and would count as methodology if solved with a guarantee (e.g., finite-sample or randomization-based coverage over the Gamma-set), but the project's own evidence suggests the intervals will be so wide at G_L<=16 and weak predictors (kidney Visium: predictions add almost nothing) that the empirical message is 'the data cannot say much', which is a poor headline. Realistic outcome: a section or application in a larger paper, or an applied-statistics / bioinformatics contribution with HEST-1k and census demos, not a standalone top-venue methods paper.

what_remains_open: Open (not found in any source searched): (1) Validity theory of cluster-level sign-change / IM-type inference for PPI and PPI++ estimators with fixed number of labelled clusters, specifically: the shared unlabelled-prediction term (common to all cluster-level estimates, a constant shift if predictions are free for all clusters), data-estimated power-tuning lambda (cross-cluster estimate induces dependence across cluster-level statistics; Hemerik-Goeman-Finos show nuisance estimation makes the basic sign-flip test conservative, so a correction would be needed), and cluster-level cross-fitting of the predictor. (2) The finite-population / without-replacement cluster-sampling design (G=14-50 total clusters, n_L=4-16 labelled): CRS/IM are superpopulation i.i.d.-cluster results with a common parameter; a design-based randomization over which clusters are labelled is a different object. I did not find a few-cluster randomization-inference paper for finite populations of clusters, only classical survey df rules (PSUs minus strata) and Lee (2010) hybrid variance estimators. (3) Heterogeneous cluster MEANS: CRS/IM/CSS validity requires the same parameter in every cluster (beta_j = beta, per the CSS text) or symmetry of the between-cluster distribution; the within-cluster CLT only makes each cluster estimate normal around its own cluster-specific rectifier mean, so with random or skewed cluster effects the cluster-level estimates are not symmetric about the target and sign-change validity fails (consistent with the project's own skewed-cluster undercoverage; Limitations of Randomization Tests in Finite Samples, arXiv:2512.07099, shows a mean-zero null admits no exact randomization test without symmetry). This last point is my reasoning from the retrieved texts, not a statement I found verbatim for PPI. (4) Power: 2^(q-1) sign patterns with q=4-8 gives p-value floors (0.125 at q=4 one-sided pattern count; CSS note size distortion bounded by 2^(1-q) and need for alpha adjustment), so with n_L=4 the level-0.05 test has zero power without randomization; that trade-off for PPI has not been analysed.
sharpened_claim_if_any: A claim that could survive: for PPI/PPI++ with a FINITE population of G clusters of which n_L are labelled (design-based, without replacement), give an interval for the finite-population (cluster-weighted or unit-weighted) estimand whose validity is proven for fixed n_L and growing cluster sizes, including (a) the cluster-level cross-fitted/estimated lambda, and (b) skewed between-cluster heterogeneity -- either via a symmetrisation/studentised-sign-flip with explicit conservativeness bound or via a t/Edgeworth correction -- accompanied by a lower bound/impossibility showing no randomization test has power at n_L<5. Plain 'apply CRS or IM to cluster-level rectified estimates' is not a claim, it is an application.
value_assessment: Blunt: as framed (sign-change/IM on cluster-level PPI estimates with a within-cluster CLT) this is a corollary of Canay-Romano-Shaikh 2017 and Ibragimov-Mueller 2016, and Broska & Howes already name it as future work, so it is better treated as a short follow-up/robustness section or software feature than as the paper. It would not by itself carry a methods paper at a top statistics journal, nor NeurIPS/ICML/AISTATS (reviewers will see 'known test, known estimator, new pairing'); an applied-methods venue (e.g. Biostatistics, a bioinformatics/spatial-omics journal) is realistic. The open remainder becomes substantive only if you prove something CRS/IM do not give: finite-population cluster design, validity with estimated lambda, and a principled treatment of skewed/heterogeneous cluster means (where the standard theory breaks and where your own empirical finding of undercoverage lives); the 2^(q-1) discreteness floor at n_L=4-6 is also a practical obstruction. There is also scooping risk: the unpublished Broska-Howes paper is 17 days old and calls out this direction.

verdict_reason: Every methodological ingredient exists in print: (i) noise-ceiling-normalised correlation and an unbiased estimator of the correlation between a model and the latent (expected) response with CIs (Hsu 2004; Schoppe 2016; Pospisil & Bair 2021, neuroscience); (ii) binomial/NB thinning of counts to evaluate arbitrary predictors with unbiased error (Batson 2019 MCV; Oliveira-Lei-Tibshirani 2025; Neufeld et al. 2024; Kawano et al. 2026 on thinning-based validation); (iii) latent-rate correlation under Poisson/NB counts with depth variation (CS-CORE 2023); (iv) a ceiling-efficiency eta=r/sqrt(rho) that re-ranks benchmark models, in genomics (single-cell perturbation preprint, 2026, unpublished). I found NO paper that applies a noise ceiling or disattenuation to histology-to-expression benchmarks (HEST-Bench etc.), none combining thinning with a correlation target, and none with donor-clustered inference; the histology literature only documents the confound empirically (Hallinan et al. 2026; Wang et al. 2025). So the application is open but the method is an assembly of known parts. Search: 73 logged queries (API + web + forward citations); the last ~3 rounds produced no new close paper. OpenAlex was not usable (see deviations).

what_remains_open: (1) The application: per-gene, per-platform noise ceiling and disattenuated correlation for HEST-Bench-style histology-to-expression evaluation on Visium/Xenium spots with re-ranked foundation models; none found (histology papers filter HVG/SVG or ablate noise). (2) Donor/slide-clustered inference for the disattenuated correlation (ratio of pooled moments, CIs with 14-24 clusters); not found for any noise-ceiling method (Pospisil-Bair assume independent trials). (3) ST specifics: neighbouring spots are not independent Poisson (diffusion, shared tissue), size factors vary by spot, overdispersion is gene-specific; whether thinning independence holds there is untested in the literature I found, and NB thinning needs known dispersion. Not open: thinning to get an independent noisy copy, the ceiling concept, CC_norm, the unbiased latent-rate correlation estimator.
sharpened_claim_if_any: With negative-binomial thinning (estimated gene-wise dispersion, spot size factors), give a consistent estimator, with donor-clustered few-cluster intervals, of the correlation between a predictor and the latent expression rate, and show how correlation-based HEST-Bench rankings change. Novelty would have to come from the clustered, overdispersed, depth-heterogeneous theory, not from thinning or the ceiling.
value_assessment: Blunt: the open remainder is thin for a top statistics journal or NeurIPS/ICML/AISTATS. Under Poisson, Var(latent)=Var(X)-E[X], so thinning is a randomised version of a closed-form errors-in-variables correction already supplied by Pospisil-Bair/CS-CORE, and thinning-based evaluation is Oliveira-Lei-Tibshirani/Neufeld/Kawano territory. What is left is application plus clustered intervals: a decent applied/benchmark note (Bioinformatics/Genome Biology style) and a useful diagnostic for your own results (your near-null Visium kidney findings may partly be a ceiling effect), but not a statistics-forward contribution unless the clustered, overdispersed, spatially dependent-noise theory yields something non-routine. Quickly scoopable. Recommend using it as a diagnostic inside the PPI project (ceiling-adjusted width ratios) rather than a standalone paper.

verdict_reason: Each of the three load-bearing components is already published, in other fields' vocabulary. (1) Randomly placed image-derived-prediction-guided sampling of fields of a tissue section with design-unbiased estimation that stays valid when the image proxy is biased is the proportionator (Gardi, Nyengaard & Gundersen 2008) and the smooth fractionator (Gundersen 2002). (2) A difference/HT estimator with inclusion probability proportional to predicted residual scale, chosen to minimise (anticipated) design variance, is Isaki-Fuller 1982 / Godambe-Joshi 1965, restated for PPI by Zrnic & Candes 2024 and, for spatial wall-to-wall predictions with a semivariogram residual model, by Shirota 2026 (Prop. 3 in v1; unpublished preprint). (3) Unit inclusion probabilities induced by random placement of a fixed-shape support (with boundary handling) are classical continuous-universe HT theory (Cordy 1993; Stevens 2000; Grafstrom 2017/2018; Mandallaz & Ye 1999 for anticipated-variance-optimal 'proportional to prediction / proportional to error' plot schemes in forest inventory). In ST itself, S2-omics (Nat Cell Biol 2025) and SpatialFinder solve the 'where to place the ROI from H&E' question purposively, with no randomisation, inclusion probabilities or valid inference, and no paper found combines ST windows with a design-unbiased estimator. So what is open is the ST instantiation plus a few technical details, not a new idea or a new estimator. Provisional: OpenAlex (and thus forward-citation search) was not available and the arXiv API returned empty responses, so coverage rests on 30 web searches plus 4 Crossref queries.

closest_papers.citation: Gardi JE, Nyengaard JR, Gundersen HJG (2008). The proportionator: unbiased stereological estimation using biased automatic image analysis and non-uniform PPS sampling. Comput Biol Med 38:313-328; and J Microsc 230:108-120.
closest_papers.how_read: abstract (plus several secondary descriptions of the method); full text not obtained
closest_papers.what_it_does: Partitions a section's region of interest into fields of view, weights each field by an image-analysis proxy for the structure, samples fields with probability proportional to weight, and obtains a design-unbiased whole-section total whatever the (biased) relation between weight and truth; efficiency depends on that relation being positive; 2-15x more efficient than systematic uniform random sampling in simulations.
closest_papers.overlap_with_claim: Essentially the whole conceptual core: cheap image-derived predictions steer random placement of expensive measurement windows, unbiasedness comes from known inclusion probabilities, efficiency from prediction quality. Not covered: expression data, residual-scale-proportional weights, difference estimator, PPI, cohort-level inference, contiguous capture areas on a spot lattice.

what_remains_open: Narrow and mostly technical. (a) The ST instantiation: randomised, HT/difference-weighted capture-area placement from H&E with valid whole-section (and cohort) inference, applied to HEST-type data; no ST paper found does this (S2-omics, SpatialFinder, iSCALE, active-spot-selection papers are all purposive or prediction-only). (b) Window-level optimisation: Isaki-Fuller/Shirota Prop. 3 optimise unit-level (or one-pixel-per-block) inclusion probabilities; choosing a density over positions of a fixed-shape contiguous window, so that unit inclusion probabilities are a convolution of the placement density with the window indicator and the anticipated variance includes within-window residual covariance, was not found stated for PPI/ST. It is, however, the Mandallaz-Ye / Cordy / Stevens machinery with the PPI residual substituted for the tree-level variable, so a derivation is likely one to two pages. (c) One-window-per-slide variance estimation (n=1 PSU per stratum; Gundersen's replicate-sampling trick, collapsed strata) combined with PPI at the cohort level: not found, but under the usual ultimate-cluster/with-replacement estimator over slides the window-placement variance is absorbed into between-slide variance automatically, which makes the within-slide piece largely unnecessary when the estimand is cohort-level with few slides. (d) Empirical question of whether foundation-model residual maps are informative enough for non-uniform placement to beat uniform on real ST: not answered in the literature found; project data (Visium kidney: predictors add almost nothing) suggest the optimal density would be near uniform there, and the ST active-selection benchmark found no consistent gain over random at small budgets.
sharpened_claim_if_any: If pursued at all: 'For a cohort-level, whole-section ST estimand with one fixed-shape capture window per slide, a design-based PPI estimator whose window-position density minimises anticipated variance under a spatial residual-covariance model that accounts for window geometry and tissue-boundary truncation, mixed with uniform for robustness, with variance from an ultimate-cluster estimator over slides; evaluated by re-windowing fully profiled large sections (e.g. HEST Xenium lung or Visium HD) rather than 6.5 mm Visium sections, which are smaller than any sensible sub-window.' Even so, the core guarantee (unbiasedness under known placement density) is inherited from stereology and survey sampling and must be credited as such.
value_assessment: Blunt: not enough on its own for a top statistics journal or NeurIPS/ICML/AISTATS methods paper. The estimator is the difference/HT estimator (Cassel et al. 1976; Mozer 2026 states PPI = difference estimator), the optimal density is Isaki-Fuller/Godambe-Joshi (restated for PPI by Zrnic-Candes and spatially by Shirota), the randomised-window-plus-biased-image-proxy idea is the proportionator, and inclusion probabilities of a randomly placed support are classical (Cordy, Stevens, Mandallaz). A reviewer who knows survey sampling, stereology or forest inventory would call it an application. What survives is (i) an applications-journal contribution (Bioinformatics / Genome Biology / Annals of Applied Statistics style) that brings design-based randomised ROI placement to ST with a retrospective re-windowing benchmark, or (ii) one section/appendix of a larger paper (e.g. 'designing which clusters/windows to label' in the PPI-with-clusters project). Risk: the empirical punchline on current data (weak histology predictors, near-uniform optimal density, no gain over random in the ST active-selection benchmark) may be that guided placement does not help, which makes a negative-result note, not a method. Do not claim novelty for unbiasedness, optimal density, or the HT/difference estimator; Shirota (unpublished, 2026) and the proportionator must be cited prominently.
